key_ideas: The book's content was shaped by the openness and stories of students who engaged in life design.
Personal relationships (specifically the authors' wives) played a foundational role in the creation of the book.
The authors express deep gratitude to the people whose support made the work possible.
This page is the table of contents for the book, listing its structural sections from Cover through Notes.
The book is organized into an Introduction, eleven numbered chapters, and a Conclusion, with the overall theme being 'Life by Design' and 'A Well-Designed Life.'
Many people choose majors and careers by default rather than by intentional design, as illustrated by Ellen choosing geology simply because she liked rocks.
Only 27 percent of college graduates in the United States end up in a career related to their majors.

The authors identify 'dysfunctional beliefs'—myths such as 'your degree determines your career' and 'college is the best four years of your life'—as obstacles that prevent people from designing the life they want.
Following a seemingly successful, planned path (college, law school, prestigious firm) does not guarantee personal fulfillment, as shown by Janine's story.
People who do not want to work in their field of study are far from alone; the assumption that a major dictates a lifelong career is a widespread but false belief.
Success and external achievement do not automatically produce happiness; a person can have everything they thought they wanted and still feel profoundly unfulfilled.
Dysfunctional beliefs—such as 'if you are successful, you will be happy' or 'it's too late'—can trap people in lives that no longer serve them.
Reframing a dysfunctional belief (e.g., 'True happiness comes from designing a life that works for you') is a step toward intentional life design.
A large portion of the workforce is unhappy: two-thirds of American workers are dissatisfied with their jobs, and 15 percent actively hate their work.
More than 31 million Americans aged 44–70 seek an 'encore' career that combines personal meaning, continued income, and social impact, yet many fear it is too late to make a change.
Designers love problems; the chapter closes by inviting the reader to look around and notice the problems in their environment as a starting point for design thinking.
Everything in our environment was designed by someone to solve a specific problem.
There is a meaningful distinction between design problems and engineering problems.
Engineering problems have a fixed, measurable goal and a single best solution that can be reproduced at scale.
Design problems have no precedent, no predetermined outcome, and multiple possible solutions that must be explored.
Aesthetics is a design problem with no single correct answer.
Aesthetics is the ultimate design problem because it involves human emotion, and design thinking is the best problem-solving tool when emotions are involved.
Designing your life is not an engineering problem with a clear goal and hard data; it is a design problem where you have a desired outcome but no clear solution in sight.
When facing a design problem, you brainstorm, try crazy stuff, improvise, and keep 'building your way forward' until something works.
A great design has a look and feel that cannot be solved with equations, spreadsheets, and data analysis.
Everything that makes daily living easier, more productive, and more enjoyable was created because a designer sought to solve a problem.
Design thinking works not just for creating products like computers and cars, but for creating a meaningful, joyful, and fulfilling life.
Anyone, regardless of age, background, or occupation, can use design thinking to solve their own life design problems.
A well-designed life is generative—it is constantly creative, productive, changing, evolving, and there is always the possibility of surprise.
In a well-designed life, you get out of it more than you put in; it is far more than 'lather, rinse, repeat.'
Discovering a fulfilling career path early is rare; most students, even at elite schools, struggle with the question of what to do with their lives.
The authors' contrasting experiences—Bill finding product design as an undergrad and Dave graduating 'for lack of a better idea'—motivated them to help others navigate career and life design.
Both authors continued working with students after starting their careers: Bill at Stanford's d.school and Dave at UC Berkeley with a course called 'How to Find Your Vocation.'

The Stanford course on designing your life originated from a single lunch meeting between Dave and Bill, who decided to partner in bringing design thinking to the problem of designing life after college.
The course applies the innovation principles of design thinking to the 'wicked problem' of designing your life at and after university.
The fundamental question of life—whether you are fifteen or fifty—is 'What do you want to be when you grow up?'
Designers love questions, but what they really love is reframing questions.
Reframing is one of the most important mind-sets of a designer.
The book exists so that anyone, not just Stanford students, can have a well-designed life.
Designers face the multidisciplinary burden of conceiving a personally meaningful, authentic, and commercially viable career vision.
Innovations get started in a reframe; in design thinking you start with people and empathy, not the problem.
A reframe (or pivot) is taking new information about the problem, restating your point of view, and thinking and prototyping again.
The biggest reframe in life design is that your life can't be perfectly planned, there isn't just one solution, and that's a good thing.
Your life is not a thing, it's an experience; the fun comes from designing and enjoying the experience.
The reframe of 'What do you want to be when you grow up?' is 'Who or what do you want to grow into?'
Life is all about growth and change; it is not static and not about a single destination.
What people need is a design process for figuring out what they want, whom they want to grow into, and how to create a life they love.
Designers imagine things that don't yet exist, build them, and the world changes; you can do this in your own life.
Even if your life is pretty perfect as is, life design can help you make it an even better version of the life you currently love living.
Life is always about designing something that has never existed before, and embracing that can make your life sparkle in unexpected ways.
No one has ever failed Stanford's Design Program class; it is impossible to flunk, and the approach has been taught to a wide range of students over decades.
The authors guarantee 'office hours for life,' meaning they remain available to students indefinitely after the course.
The course has been scientifically studied through two doctoral dissertations and proved to improve career conception, reduce dysfunctional beliefs, and increase ideation capability.
The tools and exercises in the book are proven effective, but the process is highly personal—the authors cannot generate your insights for you.
If you actually use the tools and do the life design exercises, you will generate the insights you need.
There are many versions of you, and they are all 'right'; life design helps you live into whatever version is currently relevant.
There are no wrong answers in life design, and you are not being graded.
The book contains no 'right answers'; the Try Stuff box at the end of each chapter encourages experimentation without self-measurement.
You should form a design team—a group of people who read the book and do exercises alongside you—to support one another in designing a well-designed life.
Designers are not lone geniuses working in solitude; in today's world, almost every problem requires a design team.
Radical collaboration means bringing together people with very different backgrounds so their idiosyncratic technical and human experiences generate unique solutions and empathy for end users.
d.school classes at Stanford demonstrate that cross-disciplinary teams (business, law, engineering, education, medical) produce breakthrough innovations when guided by design thinking.
Design thinking is the human-centered approach that serves as the glue holding diverse teams together, spurring collaboration and creativity.
Before you can do life design, you need to learn to think like a designer.
Designers don't think their way forward; they build their way forward by creating prototypes and trying things.
The book focuses primarily on jobs and careers because work occupies most of our waking hours and can be a source of joy or drudgery.
A well-designed life is not a life of drudgery; you are not meant to white-knuckle through a job you hate.
Five design mind-sets guide life design: curiosity, bias to action, reframing, awareness, and radical collaboration.
Curiosity makes everything new, invites exploration, and helps you 'get good at being lucky' by seeing opportunities everywhere.
Bias to action means committing to building prototypes, failing often, and embracing change rather than being attached to a particular outcome.
Reframing is how designers get unstuck from problems.
Life design involves key reframes that allow you to step back, examine your biases, and open up new solution spaces.
Reframing is essential to finding the right problems and the right solutions.
Life design is a process: mistakes will be made, prototypes thrown away, and amazing designs can emerge from the mess.
Let go of the end goal and focus on the process to see what happens next.
Radical collaboration is essential to life design; you are not alone and design is a team sport.
Most people (about 80%) do not really know what they are passionate about.
The belief that you must first discover your passion before anything else can fall into place is a dysfunctional belief.
Only one in five young people between twelve and twenty-six have a clear vision of where they want to go and what they want to accomplish.
Passion is the result of a good life design, not the cause; it develops after trying something and building mastery.
Most people do not have one singular passion; they are passionate about many different things.
You do not need to know your passion in order to design a life you love.
The way to discover what you want is to prototype potential lives, try them out, and see what resonates.
A well-designed life is one in which who you are, what you believe, and what you do all line up together.
A well-designed life is a portfolio that includes failures, hardships, adventures, and achievements.
Failures and hardships are a part of every life, even well-designed ones.
The life design process is guided by five principles: Curiosity, Bias to action, Reframing, Awareness, and Radical collaboration.
The life design process will take you out of your comfort zone and may feel counterintuitive.
"Getting good at being lucky" is a result of curiosity and awareness and a by-product of using the five mind-sets.
The process of discovering who you are and what you want has an extraordinary effect on your life, making it seem as if everyone is conspiring to help you.
There will be effort and action involved in life design, but being aware of the process makes it fun.
The book's purpose is to guide, challenge, and provide ideas and tools for designing your way through life—finding your next job, career, or big thing.
The ultimate goal is to design a life that you love.

exercises.title: Identify and Reframe a Dysfunctional Belief
exercises.purpose: To help the reader recognize a limiting belief that is keeping them stuck in an unsatisfying life and replace it with a design-oriented reframe that opens up new possibilities.
steps: Identify a dysfunctional belief you hold about your life, career, or happiness (e.g., 'If you are successful, you will be happy' or 'It's too late to make a change').
Write the belief in the form: 'Dysfunctional Belief: [your statement].'
Craft a reframe that shifts the belief toward intentional design (e.g., 'True happiness comes from designing a life that works for you' or 'It's never too late to design a life you love').
Write the reframe in the form: 'Reframe: [your new statement].'
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: If you are successful, you will be happy.
Reframe: True happiness comes from designing a life that works for you.

exercises.title: Try Stuff
exercises.purpose: To encourage readers to experiment with the book's exercises without measuring themselves against anyone, embracing the designer's mindset of iterative exploration.
steps: Work through the exercises in the book without expecting a single correct answer.
At the end of each chapter, review the Try Stuff box, which recaps the exercises covered.
Approach each exercise as a designer would: try things, iterate, and co-create rather than compete.
exercises.source_quote: We've added a recap of the exercises at the end of each chapter that has them—a Try Stuff box—because we suggest that you, well, try stuff. That's what designers do. We're not measuring you against anyone, and you shouldn't measure yourself against anyone, either.

exercises.title: Form a Design Team
exercises.purpose: To create a collaborative group that reads the book and does the exercises together, supporting one another in the pursuit of a well-designed life and embodying radical collaboration.
steps: Go out and get a design team right off the bat.
Assemble a group of people who will read the book with you and do the exercises alongside you.
Structure the group as a collaborative team in which members support one another in their pursuit of a well-designed life.
Embrace radical collaboration by including people with very different backgrounds so their idiosyncratic technical and human experiences generate unique solutions.
exercises.source_quote: we suggest you go out and get a design team right off the bat—a group of people who will read the book with you and do the exercises alongside you, a collaborative team in which you support one another in your pursuit of a welldesigned life.

key_ideas: You are where you are; it doesn't matter where you came from or where you think you should be—design thinking helps you build forward from your current position.
Designers are energized by 'wicked problems,' which are called wicked not because they are evil but because they are resistant to resolution.
Problem finding is given as much emphasis as problem solving; working on the wrong problem wastes years or a lifetime.
People often frame life problems as addition (get a better job, more money) or subtraction (get rid of pain, unhappiness), or simply as a vague sense of discontent.
Problems can become our stories, and we get stuck living with them like an irritating roommate we complain about but never evict.
Deciding which problems to work on may be one of the most important decisions a person makes.
People can remain stuck for years by working on the wrong problem, mistaking a surface-level goal for the real issue.
Career or life 'destinies' can be built on misperceptions, such as confusing a fondness for a teacher with a genuine passion for the subject they teach.
External influences like childhood heroes and charismatic teachers can create false narratives about what one is meant to do.
Trying to solve the wrong problem by doing more of the same (e.g., doing more biology research to fix a problem rooted in disliking biology) deepens the misery rather than resolving it.
The problem one thinks they are solving (becoming a marine biologist) may be entirely different from the actual problem (a misperception about one's own interests and strengths).
People often waste a lot of time working on the wrong problem, either failing quickly or falling into a 'success disaster' where they succeed at the wrong thing and end up unhappy.
A beginner's mind means approaching a problem with curiosity—asking questions, trying things, and investigating—rather than assuming you already know the answers.
Falling in love with your first idea (especially one formed by a younger, less-informed self) and refusing to let it go can derail your life for years.
It is important to regularly check in with yourself to see whether you are actually working on the right problem.
A stated 'solution' (e.g., 'I need a better job') may mask the real underlying problem (e.g., 'I'm not that happy working, and I'd rather be home with my kids').
You can waste time working on the wrong problem, such as solving a marriage problem at the office or a work problem with a new diet.
Gravity problems are not real problems because they are not actionable; they are situations, circumstances, or facts of life.
If it's not actionable, it's not a problem.
People fight reality, but reality always wins; you can't outsmart, trick, or bend it to your will.
The goal of identifying gravity problems is to free yourself from getting stuck on something that's not actionable.
Designers are first and foremost doers, so getting stuck on an inactionable issue is especially counterproductive.
There are two variations of gravity problems: totally inactionable ones (such as gravity itself) and functionally unactionable ones.

Some problems are 'gravity problems'—situations so fundamentally fixed that they are effectively inactionable (e.g., gravity itself, the median income of poets, employers' bias against long-term unemployed candidates).
You must distinguish between a gravity problem (not actionable) and a genuinely hard problem (actionable but requiring effort, sacrifice, and carrying a high risk of failure).
Accepting a gravity problem as inactionable frees your attention to design solutions to other, actionable problems.
Even in the face of daunting realities, you always have some freedom you can exercise; the strategy is to work around the gravity problem rather than against it.

Concrete alternatives exist for each gravity problem: a cyclist can lighten her bike or build stamina; a job seeker can take volunteer roles or target industries with less ageism; a poet can still promote poetry locally even if she cannot change the market.
Do not get stuck on goals you have effectively no chance of succeeding at; recognize 'gravity' problems where the structure of the situation makes the goal unattainable.
When you cannot change your life because of gravity, you can change your thinking—reframe the situation to find value in what is already available.
Look for greater value instead of greater authority; becoming the go-to expert in a high-impact function can yield more compensation and influence than a title.
Consider alternative routes that achieve a similar outcome with less time, cost, or structural constraint (e.g., physician's assistant, wellness/prevention programs).
Accepting reality with an open mind frees you to reframe an actionable problem and design a way to participate in the world on things that matter to you.
Pursue aggressive, world-changing goals, but do it smart—choose problems you can actually influence rather than ones locked behind institutional gravity.
Acceptance is the only response to a gravity problem and the starting point for all good design.
You must start where you are—not where you wish, hope, or think you should be.
Life can be broken into four discrete areas: health, work, play, and love.
Health means being well in mind, body, and spirit (emotional, physical, and mental health).
Work is broader than paid employment; it is your participation in the great ongoing human adventure on the planet.
Play is any activity done purely for the joy of doing it, not to win, advance, or achieve.
The Life Design Assessment is a way to take stock of your situation and answer 'How's it going?' across all four areas.
Understanding how work fits into the rest of your life is necessary before you can design your work.
You can't know where you're going until you know where you are.
Love comes in a wide range of types (affection, community, eroticism) and from a huge array of sources (parents, friends, colleagues, lovers), but all share a sense of connection.
There is no appraisal or judgment of your life in the four areas; everyone has needed a remodel in at least one.
Awareness and curiosity are the design mind-sets needed to begin building your way forward.
Health is the foundation: when you're not healthy, nothing else in your life works very well.
There is no perfect balance of health, work, play, and love; the appropriate mix changes with life stage.
The dysfunctional belief 'I should already know where I'm going' should be reframed as 'You can't know where you are going until you know where you are.'
Health encompasses more than a doctor's checkup; it includes a healthy body, an engaged mind, and often some form of spiritual practice.
'Spiritual' does not necessarily mean religious; it refers to any practice based on a belief in something bigger than ourselves.
There is no objective perfect balance across life areas, only a subjective personal sense of 'I have enough' or 'Something is missing.'
The life dashboard functions like an emergency light on a car's dashboard, serving as an indicator that it is time to pull over and figure out what is wrong.
The relative importance of each health area (body, mind, spirit) is entirely up to the individual.
A well-designed life is supported by balance across multiple categories such as health, play, love, and work.
You can assess the quality of your life by rating different areas (Health, Work, Play, Love) on a gauge from quarter full to really full.
How you rate your health factors significantly into how you assess the quality of your life and what you might want to redesign going forward.
Work includes all forms of labor: paid jobs, second jobs, consulting, volunteering, and homemaking (raising children, cooking, caring for aging parents, housework).
Play is activity that brings joy for the pure sake of the doing of it, not for merit, and all lives need some play.
Love arrives in a wide range of forms—primary relationship, children, people, pets, community—and it is critical to feel loved by others.
A low gauge in any area (e.g., Bill's 'red light' on Play) signals a part of life that may need redesigning.
Love must flow in both directions—both from you and from others.
The health/work/play/love dashboard provides a single framework and data snapshot of your life's current status.
Life design is an iterative process of prototypes and experimentation; life is never done until you die.
Red lights on the dashboard (e.g., low play, poor health) flag areas that need attention.
Balance and proportionality across the four areas matter, but perfect symmetry is neither expected nor required.
Before tackling a wicked problem, check first for a 'gravity problem' and ask whether the problem is actionable.
It is impossible to predict the future, but once you design something, it changes the future that is possible.
Designing something changes the future that is possible.
You cannot know your future or figure out a great life design before you begin, but you do have a good idea of your starting point.
You need a compass to get pointed in the right direction for the journey ahead.
Life can be assessed across four areas: Health, Work, Play, and Love.
It is important to distinguish between a design problem (one you can tackle) and a gravity problem (one you cannot change).

exercises.title: The Life Design Assessment
exercises.purpose: To take stock of your current situation by breaking life into discrete areas (health, work, play, and love) and producing an articulated characterization of where you are, answering the question 'How's it going?'
steps: Break your life down into the four discrete areas: health, work, play, and love.

Define how you will measure each area. For health, decide what 'healthy' means to you across mind, body, and spirit, and how you will measure it. For work, consider all forms of work, not just paid employment. For play, identify activities that bring you joy purely in the doing. For love, reflect on your relationships.
Take your own inventory of each area—examine your current situation honestly.
Make an assessment: produce an articulated characterization of where you are in each area.
Answer the question 'How's it going?' for each of the four areas.
exercises.source_quote: In order to start where we are, we need to break life down into some discrete areas —health, work, play, and love.

exercises.title: Health Work Play / Love Dashboard
exercises.purpose: To take stock of your current situation—your 'You Are Here'—by assessing the four areas that provide energy and focus for your journey, so you can identify which design problem to tackle first.
steps: Think of the four areas (health, work, play, love) like the gauges on your car's dashboard, each telling you something about the state of your life.
Assess your state of health, recognizing it as the base of the diagram because when you're not healthy, nothing else works very well.
Assess the ways you work, noting that work is built on top of health.
Assess the ways you play, noting that play is built on top of health.
Assess the ways you love, considering the range of types (affection, community, eroticism) and sources (parents, friends, colleagues, lovers) and the sense of connection each provides.
Recognize that there is no perfect balance; identify the mix that is appropriate for you at your current stage of life.
Figure out what design problem you'd like to tackle first based on your assessment.
exercises.source_quote: The exercise below is going to help you figure out where you are and what design problem you'd like to tackle. You can't know where you're going until you know where you are.

exercises.title: The Life Dashboard Assessment
exercises.purpose: To identify areas of life that are out of balance or missing, using a visual diagram as an early-warning indicator, much like an emergency light on a car's dashboard.
steps: Look at the dashboard diagram with its categories (e.g., health, play, love, work).
Review your entries in each category to see where you have invested time and energy.
Identify any 'red lights'—categories where you have almost no entries or where something feels missing.
Decide whether the imbalance is acceptable to you (as Fred did with play) or whether it requires change (as Fred did with health).
Make concrete changes in the areas flagged as out of balance.
materials: The dashboard diagram with life categories (health, play, love, work, etc.)
exercises.source_quote: a look at this diagram can sometimes warn us that something is not right. Like an emergency light on your car's dashboard, the diagram may serve as an indicator that it's time to pull over and figure out what's wrong.

exercises.title: Your Health Gauge
exercises.purpose: To make a quick, personal assessment of your overall well-being across body, mind, and spirit, and to record where you stand on the gauge.
steps: Consider your health in terms of body, mind, and spirit (not just a physical checkup).
Determine the relative importance of each area (body, mind, spirit) for yourself.
Make a quick assessment of your current health in those areas.
Fill in your gauge to reflect where you stand.

exercises.title: Health Gauge
exercises.purpose: To help you honestly assess your physical and mental health so you can identify what you might want to redesign going forward.
steps: Consider your overall physical and mental health, including recent medical results, exercise habits, cognitive function, spiritual practices, and community support.
Rate your health on a gauge: quarter full, half, three-quarters, or really full.
Write a short paragraph describing the specifics behind your rating (as Bill does in his example, noting both positives and areas of concern).
materials: Paper or notebook for writing your rating and description
Bill's dashboard example for reference
exercises.source_quote: How you rate your health will factor significantly into how you assess the quality of your life and what you might want to redesign going forward.

exercises.title: Work Gauge
exercises.purpose: To help you take inventory of all the ways you 'work'—paid, unpaid, and domestic—and then assess your overall working life.
steps: Make a list of all the ways you 'work,' including your nine-to-five job, any second job, consulting or advising, regular volunteering, and (if applicable) homemaking tasks such as raising children, providing home-cooked meals, taking care of aging parents, and doing housework.
Gauge your working life as a whole: quarter full, half, three-quarters, or really full.
Write a short description of your work situation (as in Bill's example listing his Stanford job, private consulting, workshops, and board service).
materials: Paper or notebook for listing and rating
exercises.source_quote: Make a list of all the ways you "work," and then "gauge" your working life as a whole.

exercises.title: Play Gauge
exercises.purpose: To help you identify the activities in your life that bring joy for the pure sake of doing them and assess whether you have enough play.
steps: Make a quick list of how you play—activities done for fun and not merit, whether organized or productive.
Fill in your gauge: are you a quarter full, or half, or three-quarters, or really full?
Note if your rating is a 'red light' on your dashboard, signaling an area that may need attention.
materials: Paper or notebook for listing and rating
exercises.source_quote: Make a quick list of how you play and then fill in your gauge— are you a quarter full, or half, or three-quarters, or really full?

exercises.title: Love Gauge
exercises.purpose: To help you assess the love in your life across its many forms—primary relationship, children, friends, pets, community—and recognize where you may need to pay more attention.
steps: Consider the various forms love takes in your life: your primary relationship first, then children, then the wider circle of people, pets, community, and other objects of affection.
Rate your love gauge: quarter full, half, three-quarters, or really full.
materials: Paper or notebook for rating
exercises.source_quote: We do think that love makes the world go around, and when we don't have any, our world isn't as bright and alive as it could be.

exercises.title: Love List and Gauge
exercises.purpose: To identify where love is flowing in your life—both outward and inward—and to rate that area on your dashboard gauge.
steps: Reflect on where love is flowing in your life, from you and from others.
Make a list of the people, activities, art, music, spaces, or other things you love and that love you back.
Fill in your Love gauge on the dashboard based on that list.
materials: Dashboard/gauge tool (from the workbook)
Paper or notebook for the list
exercises.source_quote: Where is the love flowing in your life, from you and from others? Make a list, and then fill in your gauge.

exercises.title: Dashboard Re-Check
exercises.purpose: To revisit your health/work/play/love dashboard after working through additional chapters and tools, and to notice whether anything has shifted.
steps: After completing a few more chapters and tools, return to your dashboard assessment.
Re-evaluate each gauge (health, work, play, love) and note any changes.
Ask yourself: Are you happy right now with where your gauges stand in each of these four areas?
Ask yourself: Have you looked at them honestly?
Ask yourself: Are there areas that need action?
Ask yourself: Have you perhaps come up against one of your wicked problems?
materials: Completed dashboard/gauge tool
exercises.source_quote: After a few more chapters and a few more tools and ideas, you may want to come back to this assessment and check the dashboard one more time, to see if anything has changed.

exercises.title: Gravity Problem Check
exercises.purpose: To determine whether a perceived 'wicked problem' is actually a gravity problem (unactionable) before investing design effort into it.
steps: If you suspect you have hit a wicked problem, pause.
Check first for a 'gravity problem'—a constraint that cannot be changed or acted upon.
Ask yourself whether the problem is actionable.
Only proceed with design work if the problem is actionable.
exercises.source_quote: If you think you have, make sure to check first for a "gravity problem." Ask yourself if your problem is actionable.

exercises.title: Balance and Proportionality Review
exercises.purpose: To examine whether your four dashboard areas show a reasonable expression of balance and proportionality, without expecting perfect symmetry.
steps: Look at your completed dashboard as a whole.
Look for some expression of balance and proportionality across health, work, play, and love.
Do not imagine that there is some perfect symmetry or balance between all the areas.
Recognize that the four areas are unlikely to divide neatly into four equal parts.
Note whether life is 'really out of balance' in a way that signals a problem.
materials: Completed dashboard/gauge tool
exercises.source_quote: Also, look for some expression of balance and proportionality in your dashboard—very important for design—without imagining that there is some perfect symmetry or balance between all the areas in your life.

exercises.title: Health Work Play / Love Dashboard
exercises.purpose: To help the reader take stock of their current state across four key life areas, identify a design problem they would like to tackle, and determine whether that problem is a solvable design problem or an unchangeable gravity problem.
steps: Write a few sentences about how it's going in each of the four areas (Health, Work, Play, Love).
Mark where you are (0 to Full) on each gauge.
Ask yourself if there's a design problem you'd like to tackle in any of these areas.
Now ask yourself if your "problem" is a gravity problem.
materials: Health Work Play / Love Dashboard (with gauges marked 0 to Full)
exercises.source_quote: Write a few sentences about how it's going in each of the four areas.

key_ideas: Worry, analysis, and speculation are not effective discovery tools for figuring out your life; they keep you spinning in circles.
Obsessing about your life is not the same as designing your life.
Life design is a way to figure out your own answers to perennial questions such as 'What is the good life?' and 'What is my purpose?'
Building a compass requires two components: a Workview and a Lifeview.
A Workview is your personal philosophy of work—what work is for and why you do it.
Articulating your own Workview makes you less likely to let others design your life for you.
The life design dashboard (completed in the previous chapter) is the first step in designing your life; building the compass is the next step.
Everyone has a Lifeview—simply your ideas about the world, what gives life meaning, and how your life relates to others.
Your Workview and Lifeview together form your personal compass for a well-designed life.
Your Workview and Lifeview will change over a lifetime; you only need the compass for what life is about for you right now.
There is a risk of accidentally using someone else's compass and living someone else's life by emulating powerful external models.
The best way to avoid living someone else's life is to clearly articulate your own Workview and Lifeview.
The goal of a well-designed life is coherency: clearly connecting who you are, what you believe, and what you are doing.
There is often a gap between what you believe and what you do, leading to disappointment and discontent.
Trade-offs and compromises are inevitable, but making them as conscious decisions keeps you coherent and on course.
Living coherently does not mean everything is in perfect order; it means living in alignment with your values without sacrificing integrity.
A good compass lets you see connections between who you are, what you believe, and what you are doing, so you can recognize when you are on course, in tension, or in need of course correction.
Connecting these three dots increases your sense of self, helps you create more meaning, and leads to greater satisfaction.
The current quest is to design your life, not to find the Holy Grail.
A Workview is a general statement of your view of work—your definition of what good work deserves to be—not merely a list of what you want from a job.
A Workview is a relatively new idea for most people, and getting stuck on the exercise often means the writer is listing job preferences rather than articulating a philosophical view of work.
Work is often the largest single component of most people's waking lives, occupying more attention and energy than anything else over a lifetime.
Your Workview is your philosophy of work—what it's for and what it means—and it is essentially your work manifesto.
Workviews can range widely, addressing service to others, money, standard of living, growth, learning, skills, and talents.
Martin Seligman found that people who connect their work to something socially meaningful are more likely to find satisfaction and adapt to work-related stresses.
Your compass won't be complete without your Workview.
Your Lifeview provides your definition of 'matters of ultimate concern'—what matters most to you.
Design is values-neutral; the philosophical and spiritual questions are given to provoke thought, not to take sides.
There are no wrong Lifeviews; the only way to do this incorrectly is not to do it at all.
Be curious and think like a designer when exploring your Lifeview questions.
Integrating your Workview and Lifeview produces the biggest 'aha' moments and increases clarity and coherence.
Your articulated and integrated Lifeview and Workview together constitute your 'True North'—your compass.
Life is not a straight line; you tack according to conditions, and sometimes storms hit and you get lost.
Compass calibration should be done at least once a year or during any major transition.
Before starting a new situation or pursuing something new, check your compass and orient yourself.
The dysfunctional belief 'I should know where I'm going!' is a barrier to the ongoing quest of finding your way.
You don't need to know your exact destination; you only need to know whether you're going in the right direction.
Your Workview and Lifeview are separate but interconnected frameworks that shape how you navigate life.
Examining where your work and life views complement, clash, or drive one another helps you build a personal compass.

exercises.title: Writing Your Lifeview
exercises.purpose: To articulate your personal ideas about the world and how it works, forming one half of your life compass and ensuring you are not living by someone else's values.
steps: Reflect on what gives life meaning to you.
Consider what makes your life worthwhile or valuable.
Examine how your life relates to others in your family, your community, and the world.
Evaluate what money, fame, and personal accomplishment have to do with a satisfying life for you.
Assess how important experience, growth, and fulfillment are in your life.
Write your answers into a coherent statement of your Lifeview.
exercises.source_quote: A Lifeview is simply your ideas about the world and how it works. What gives life meaning? What makes your life worthwhile or valuable? How does your life relate to others in your family, your community, and the world? What do money, fame, and personal accomplishment have to do with a satisfying life? How important are experience, growth, and fulfillment in your life?

exercises.title: Writing Your Workview
exercises.purpose: To articulate your personal beliefs about work, forming the other half of your life compass alongside your Lifeview.
steps: Write out your Workview, articulating your ideas about what work means to you and how you want to engage with it.
exercises.source_quote: Once you've written your Workview and your Lifeview, and completed the simple exercise that follows, you'll have your compass and be on the path toward a well-designed life.

exercises.title: Workview Reflection
exercises.purpose: To help the reader articulate a fundamental, philosophical view of what work is and what it means to them, moving beyond a simple list of job preferences toward a coherent personal definition of good and worthwhile work.
steps: Write a short reflection about your Workview. Do not do it in your head; actually write it down.
Set aside about thirty minutes for the exercise.
Aim for approximately 250 words—less than a page of typed writing.
Write a general statement of your view of work, not just a list of what you want from or out of work.

Address critical issues related to what work is and what it means to you, considering questions such as: Why work? What's work for? What does work mean? How does it relate to the individual, others, society? What defines good or worthwhile work? What does money have to do with it? What do experience, growth, and fulfillment have to do with it?
Frame your reflection as your definition of what good work deserves to be.
materials: Paper and pen, or a computer for typing (the text references 'less than a page of typed writing')
exercises.source_quote: Write a short reflection about your Workview. We're not looking for a term paper here (and we're still not grading you), but we do want you really to write this down. Don't do it in your head. This should take about thirty minutes. Try to shoot for 250 words—less than a page of typed writing.

exercises.title: Workview Reflection
exercises.purpose: To reflect on and articulate your philosophy of work—why you work, what work and vocation mean to you, and what you hope work means for others—producing a personal work manifesto.
steps: Reflect on why you work, not what work you want to do.
Consider the broadest definition of work, not just paid employment.
Think about what work and vocation mean to you, and perhaps what you hope work means for others.
Address the issues you think are important, such as service to others, money and standard of living, growth, learning, skills, and talents.
Consider whether you want to make an explicit connection between your work and something socially meaningful.
Write down your Workview.
exercises.source_quote: For this exercise, we're not interested in what work you want to do, but why you work.

exercises.title: Lifeview Reflection
exercises.purpose: To write down the critical defining values and perspectives that provide the basis for your understanding of life—your 'matters of ultimate concern.'
steps: Write a reflection on your Lifeview, taking no more than thirty minutes.
Aim for approximately 250 words.

Address questions such as: Why are we here? What is the meaning or purpose of life? What is the relationship between the individual and others? Where do family, country, and the rest of the world fit in? What is good, and what is evil? Is there a higher power, God, or something transcendent, and if so, what impact does this have on your life? What is the role of joy, sorrow, justice, injustice, love, peace, and strife in life?
Write down whatever critical defining values and perspectives provide the basis for your understanding of life.
exercises.source_quote: Just as you did with the Workview, please write a reflection on your Lifeview. This should also take no more than thirty minutes and be 250 words or so.

exercises.title: Writing Down Your Lifeview Answers
exercises.purpose: To articulate your personal Lifeview by reflecting on and answering questions that matter to you, treating the process as a design exercise rather than a debate.
steps: Review the Lifeview questions and decide which ones you want to try to answer.
Be curious and think like a designer; ask the questions that work for you and make up your own.
See what you discover through your answers.
Write down your answers.
materials: Paper or notebook for writing down answers
exercises.source_quote: Write down your answers. Ready. Begin.

exercises.title: Coherency and Workview-Lifeview Integration
exercises.purpose: To examine how your Workview and Lifeview complement, clash, or drive one another, and to edit them so they are in harmony, increasing your ability to live a consciously coherent, meaningful life.
steps: Read over your Workview and Lifeview.
Write down your thoughts on where your views on work and life complement one another.
Write down your thoughts on where they clash.
Write down your thoughts on whether one drives the other, and how.
Take time to write up your thoughts on the integration of your two views.
Edit one or both of your views as the reflection reveals misalignments.

Your existing Lifeview document
Paper or notebook for writing

exercises.title: Compass Calibration
exercises.purpose: To reorient yourself by verifying that your Workview and Lifeview still align with your current life, especially during transitions, new pursuits, or when you feel your life is not working.
steps: Double-check your Workview and Lifeview.
Make sure they align with each other and with your current situation.
Perform this calibration at least once a year.

Your Lifeview document

exercises.purpose: To help the reader articulate their underlying views on work and on life, then examine how those two views interact—complementing, clashing, or driving one another—as a step toward building a personal compass.
steps: Write a short reflection about your Workview. Aim for about 250 words (less than a page of typed writing); allow roughly thirty minutes.
Write a short reflection about your Lifeview. Again aim for about 250 words and allow no more than thirty minutes.

key_ideas: Following others' plans for your career and life can create a false sense of direction until the plan stops working, leaving you feeling lost.
The dysfunctional belief that 'work is not supposed to be enjoyable' should be reframed: enjoyment is a guide to finding the right work for you.
Wayfinding is the ancient art of figuring out where you are going when you don't actually know your destination.
Having an articulated Lifeview and Workview is essential; without them, you let other people steer your course.
External advice (from friends, family, in-laws) often reflects the advisor's assumptions rather than the person's own direction.
Wayfinding your life means paying attention to the clues in front of you and making your best way forward, rather than following a predetermined map or GPS-style plan.
Engagement and energy are the first clues to pay attention to when wayfinding your life.
Designers have a bias to action, meaning they pay attention to doing things rather than just thinking about them.
Flow is engagement on steroids: a state in which time stands still, you are totally engaged, and the challenge of the activity matches your skill so you are neither bored nor anxious.
Flow was discovered by Professor Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, who studied the detailed activities of thousands of people going about their daily lives.
Flow is characterized by feelings of ecstasy, great inner clarity, total calm, and a distortion of time.
Flow can occur during almost any physical or mental activity and is a qualitative experience you must identify for yourself.
Flow is 'play for grown-ups'—the essence of play is being fully immersed and joyful without distraction from concerns about outcomes.
A really rewarding and satisfying career involves a lot of flow states, and flow should be a regular part of work, home, exercise, and love life.
Energy is the second wayfinding clue after engagement.
The brain represents about 2 percent of body weight but consumes 25 percent of daily energy (roughly 500 of 2,000 calories).
How we invest our attention is critical to whether we feel high or low energy.
Some activities sustain our energy and some drain it; tracking those energy flows is important.
Life design is primarily about tuning up and improving the life you're in, not making huge structural changes like changing jobs or moving.
Engagement and energy are related but distinct: high engagement does not always coincide with high energy.
Energy can go negative—some activities can drain you completely, sending you depleted into whatever comes next.
Boredom is an energy-suck but is much easier to recover from than being de-energized by a draining activity.
Paying detailed attention to what energizes and drains you can reveal that you actually enjoy your work, and the problem lies in specific tasks rather than the whole job.
You can craft your role to do more of what you love and less of what you hate, without leaving your field entirely.
Follow the joy; follow what engages and excites you and brings you alive.
Work is fun when you are leaning into your strengths and are deeply engaged and energized by what you're doing—not from parties, money, or vacations.
You will spend 90,000 to 125,000 hours working over your lifetime, so if most of it isn't bringing you alive, a lot of your life will suffer.
Purpose and mission matter, but focused attention on engagement and energy level provides very helpful clues to wayfinding your path forward.
Life design consists of a whole set of ideas and tools that work together flexibly; you decide which to focus on and how to organize your project.
The Good Time Journal has two elements: an Activity Log (recording where you're engaged and energized) and Reflections (discovering what you are learning).
Log your primary activities daily (or at least twice a week) along with how engaged and energized you felt, to build a rich dataset about what motivates you.
Most people do not pay detailed attention to the specific moments that make a day good or bad; the practice is to drill down into the particulars and catch yourself in the act of having a good time.
The Good Time Journal has two elements: the Activity Log (data collection) and weekly reflection (pattern recognition).
Complete the Activity Log for at least three weeks before reflecting, so you capture all the various kinds of activities that arise in your current situation.
Weekly reflection should look for trends, insights, and surprises that reveal what does and doesn't work for you.
Identify activities that reliably create flow states and activities that return more energy than they consume, then adjust your schedule to surround less engaging activities with more engaging ones.
Energy-negative activities should be done when you are well rested so you can do them right the first time, avoiding the extra cost of redoing them.
Journaling about a draining activity can reveal specific, fixable causes such as a poor environment or an ineffective interaction structure.
Redesigning the environment and structure of a draining task based on journal insights can transform it into a source of flow.

The Good Time Journal can serve different strategic purposes—improving your current life design or identifying a career path—while using the same core technique of paying detailed attention to what is engaging and energizing you.
Zooming in on journal entries to capture the precise activity or behavior that engaged you leads to more insightful reflections and a clearer wayfinding direction.
Asking specific either/or questions during reflection (e.g., 'Was I more engaged by X or by Y?') sharpens self-awareness about what truly drives engagement.
Identifying the 'sweet spot' of a positive experience (e.g., artful articulation vs. group facilitation) helps you seek out matching future opportunities.
The AEIOU method (Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects, Users) is a structured observation tool borrowed from design to make detailed, accurate reflections on your Activity Log.
Environment has a profound effect on emotional state; noticing where you were and how the place made you feel is a key part of self-observation.
Zooming in on specific details of an experience helps you discover precisely what is or isn't working for you.
Take journal reflection as far as you find helpful and no further—you don't want to get stuck in your journal.
The AEIOU method supports developing a curiosity mind-set by prompting you to look at experiences from multiple angles.
The AEIOU method (Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects, Users) helps extract more insight from Good Time Journal observations.
When reflecting in the Good Time Journal, record whatever comes up without judging yourself; there are no right or wrong feelings.
Past peak experiences ('mountaintop moments') contain valuable insights that can be mined for life-design purposes.
Writing peak experiences as a list or narrative makes it easier to extract the activities that most engaged and energized you.

A historical Good Time Journal on past non-work projects (school, volunteer work, summer programs) is useful when current work doesn't lend itself to the exercise or when you are early in your career.
When looking back at past experiences, beware of revisionist history—be honest rather than too kind to good days or too critical of bad times.
Environment alone may not be enough for long-term satisfaction; the specific role (interactions, objects, users) matters as well.
Noticing how things make YOU feel, rather than how your mom, dad, boss, or spouse would feel, is a shift to a new level of awareness.
Wayfinding means moving from where you are to the next possible place, mapping territory already covered and seeing new possibilities ahead.
Armed with your compass and Good Time Journal insights, you can effectively wayfind.
The next step in wayfinding is to generate as many options as possible so you have lots to experiment with and prototype.
Mind mapping is the tool introduced for generating options.

exercises.title: Good Time Journal
exercises.purpose: To help you catch yourself in the act of having a good time and discover what activities reliably engage you, so you can articulate something helpful for your life design work.

Continue this daily logging assignment for a few weeks.

Identify which activities sustain your energy and which drain it.
Track those energy flows as part of your wayfinding process.

exercises.purpose: To help readers identify which weekly activities energize or drain them so they can redesign their activities to maximize vitality within their current life.
steps: Track where your energy goes every week, paying specific attention to your energy levels (not just engagement).
Distinguish between engagement and energy: note times when you were engaged but still drained, or bored but not particularly de-energized.
Identify activities that raise your energy and those that lower it, including activities that send your energy negative.

exercises.title: Good Time Journal
exercises.purpose: To track where you are engaged and energized in your daily life and to reflect on what you are learning, providing concrete clues for wayfinding your career and life path forward.
steps: Choose a format that you will most enjoy and use most often: a bound journal, a three-ring binder with loose sheets, or a computer (hand is strongly recommended so you can sketch).
Make entries regularly; the most important thing is that you actually do it.
Maintain an Activity Log in which you record where you are engaged and energized.
Write Reflections in which you discover what you are learning.

exercises.purpose: To capture detailed, ongoing data about which activities engage and energize you, building the raw material needed to identify your most motivating work activities with specificity.
steps: List your primary activities for the day.
For each activity, rate how engaged you were (using a gauge or symbol).
For each activity, rate how energized you were (using a gauge or symbol).
Make entries daily, or at minimum twice a week, to avoid missing too much information.

exercises.purpose: To review accumulated Activity Log data and identify trends, insights, and surprises that reveal which activities energize you, which drain you, and how to adjust your schedule accordingly.
steps: Ensure you have completed Activity Log entries for at least three weeks.
Look over your Activity Log entries.
Notice trends, insights, and surprises—anything that is a clue to what does and doesn't work for you.
Identify activities that reliably create flow states.
Identify activities that return significantly more energy than they consume.
Note activities that drain energy (e.g., budget meetings) and any that are variable (e.g., faculty meetings that are sometimes interesting, sometimes not).
Write your reflections on blank pages in your Good Time Journal.
Adjust your schedule to surround less engaging activities with more engaging ones, or to double up on energizing activities.

exercises.title: Zooming In on Good Time Journal Entries
exercises.purpose: To move from vague log entries to precise descriptions of the specific activity or behavior that engaged you, so your reflections become more insightful and your wayfinding direction is clearer.
steps: After a week or two of keeping your Good Time Journal, review your accumulated entries.
Identify entries that feel too general or vague (e.g., 'Staff Mtg—Enjoyed it for once today!').

Restate each selected entry with greater precision, specifying the exact activity or behavior that produced the positive feeling (e.g., 'Staff Mtg—Felt great when I rephrased what Jon said and everyone went "Ooooh—exactly!"').

When journaling your reflection on the restated entry, ask yourself a specific either/or question to isolate what truly engaged you (e.g., 'Was I more engaged by artfully rephrasing Jon's comment or by facilitating consensus among the staff?').
Use the sharper detail in your entries to set a more precise wayfinding direction.
materials: Good Time Journal (notebook or digital journal with at least a week or two of entries)
exercises.source_quote: After a week or two, when you've got a decent body of entries in your Good Time Journal and you're starting to notice some interesting things, it's time to zoom in and take the exercise to the next level.

exercises.title: Journaling to Diagnose Energy-Draining Activities
exercises.purpose: To uncover the specific, fixable causes (such as environment or interaction structure) behind an activity that drains your energy, so you can redesign it and reduce its energy cost.
steps: Identify an activity that is draining your energy (an 'energy-negative' task).
Journal specifically about that activity, examining what is going wrong.
Look for concrete, fixable causes—for example, a poor physical environment or an ineffective interaction structure.
Redesign the activity based on what you discovered (e.g., change the location, shift from one-on-one to small-group format).
Monitor the redesigned activity over the following weeks to see whether it now produces flow or at least feels more bearable.
materials: Good Time Journal or any notebook for journaling
exercises.source_quote: After journaling a bit on that subject, he discovered two things: (1) he was trying to coach in a bad environment (the noisy graduate studio) and (2) his coaching interaction wasn't effective—his students weren't "getting it."

exercises.title: Good Time Journal Reflection on a Unifying Moment
exercises.purpose: To identify the specific 'sweet spot' of a positive experience and use that insight to guide you toward matching future opportunities (e.g., content-creation vs. group facilitation).
steps: Recall a unifying moment from a positive experience (e.g., a staff meeting).
Ask yourself what the real sweet spot of that moment was for you (e.g., artful articulation, group facilitation, brainstorming).
Conclude which element was the true source of your engagement.
Use that insight to be on the lookout for opportunities that match your identified sweet spot.
Take the observation and reflection as far as you find helpful and no further—avoid getting stuck in your journal.
materials: Journal (implied by the instruction not to get stuck in your journal)
exercises.source_quote: If you conclude that artful articulation was the real sweet spot of that staff meeting moment for you, that important insight can help you be on the lookout for content-creation opportunities over group facilitation opportunities.

exercises.title: AEIOU Observation Method
exercises.purpose: To make detailed and accurate observations when reflecting on your Activity Log, helping you zoom in effectively and discover specifically what is or isn't working for you.
steps: Activities: Ask what you were actually doing. Was it structured or unstructured? Did you have a specific role (team leader) or were you just a participant?
Environments: Notice where you were. What kind of place was it, and how did it make you feel?
Interactions: Ask what you were interacting with—people or machines. Was it a new kind of interaction or familiar? Was it formal or informal?
Objects: Identify any objects or devices you were interacting with (iPads, smartphones, hockey sticks, sailboats). What objects created or supported your feeling engaged?
Users: Note who else was there and what role they played in making it a positive or negative experience.
Use the observations across all five categories to zoom in on what specifically is or isn't working for you.
materials: Activity Log (the log you are reflecting on)
exercises.source_quote: It's the AEIOU method3 that provides you five sets of questions you can use when reflecting on your Activity Log.

exercises.title: Good Time Journal with AEIOU Method

steps: Work on your reflections in the Good Time Journal.
Apply the AEIOU method to categorize your observations into Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects, and Users.
Record whatever comes up without judging yourself; there are no right or wrong feelings about your experience.
Focus on the fact that this information will be incredibly helpful in designing your life.

exercises.source_quote: As you work on your reflections in the Good Time Journal, try using this AEIOU method to get more out of your observations. It is important to record whatever comes up and not to judge yourself—there are no right or wrong feelings about your experience.

Do a Good Time Journal Activity Log and reflection on those peak experiences.
Make a list of those peak experiences, or write them out as a narrative or story.
Extract from those stories the activities that most engaged and energized you.
Discover insights from the narratives that you can apply today.

exercises.source_quote: Take some time to reflect on your memories of past peak work-related experiences and do a Good Time Journal Activity Log and reflection on them to see what you find.

exercises.purpose: To apply the Good Time Journal method to past non-work experiences (school projects, volunteer work, summer programs) when you are between jobs, early in your career, or lack current work experience to draw from.
steps: Think about activities you did in other areas of your life (perhaps even decades ago) when you felt that life was working.
Do a historical Good Time Journal on past projects from school, summer programs, volunteer projects—anything you were seriously engaged by.
Beware of revisionist history: avoid being too kind to the good days or too critical of the bad times.
Try to be honest in your recollections.

exercises.purpose: To build awareness of which activities genuinely engage and energize you, providing the data needed to wayfind toward your next direction.
