key_ideas: You are never truly stuck because you can always generate a large number of ideas.
Designers know you never go with your first idea; you generate many options first.
When you choose from lots of options, you choose better.
Many people get stuck by trying to make their first idea work instead of exploring alternatives.
The belief 'I'm stuck' is a dysfunctional belief that can be reframed.
Thinking like a designer—generating many possibilities before choosing—is the antidote to feeling trapped in a single path.
Doing the 'right thing' (e.g., following conventional career advice) does not guarantee happiness; you must do what is right for you.
Looking at job listings and picking a job you think you can get is one of the worst ways to find work and has the lowest success rate.
Being stuck is not a failure state; it can be a launching pad for creativity.
You cannot know what you want until you know what you might want, so you must generate a large volume of ideas and possibilities.
Believing there is only one correct idea creates pressure and indecision; ideation means producing many wild, crazy options.
Designers get stuck all the time and use ideation to 'flare' out into many possible futures.
The modern obsession with optimization—always seeking the one best idea or best way—is dangerous to life design.
Each person has multiple lives in them (the average answer to 'how many lifetimes' worth of living are in you?' is 3.4), and there are many valid, happy, productive paths to live.
Quantity has a quality all its own: more ideas equal access to better ideas, and better ideas lead to a better design.
The number one enemy of creativity is judgment; the brain's critical wiring can silently imprison the majority of ideas behind a wall of premature judgment.
Designers ideate broadly and wildly, embracing crazy ideas as much as sensible ones, because deferring judgment and silencing the inner critic allows the full range of ideas to surface.
Getting out into the 'wild idea space' is the sign that premature judgment has been overcome.
Embracing crazy ideas moves you into a new creative space where innovative possibilities become visible.
You choose better when you have lots of good ideas to choose from.
You never choose your first solution to any problem; first ideas are typically average and not very creative.
The mind is lazy and surrounds first ideas with positive chemicals to make you 'fall in love' with them, creating a bias toward the obvious.
Creativity is innate (evident in early childhood) but is often suppressed by negative feedback from adults and social norms.
Mind mapping is an ideation technique that uses free association of words to open up the idea space and generate new solutions.
Mind mapping is a visual method that bypasses the inner logical/verbal censor, allowing ideas and their associations to be captured automatically.
The technique teaches you to generate lots of ideas by free-associating in rings of word connections.
Words in outer rings only need to be associated to the word in the previous ring, not to the central topic.
A time limit of three to five minutes keeps the process fast and prevents the inner censor from interfering.
The outer perimeter of the mind map contains ideas two or three steps away from conscious thinking, making them the most creative and unexpected.
Mashing random words from the outer layer together creates new concepts that feel disconnected but are linked in the unconscious back to the original prompt.
Innovation comes from taking individual components and mashing them up into new, combined ideas.
It is not about finding the perfect job; it is about making the job you have 'perfect.'
Your current job can serve as a springboard to what's next.
When generating ideas, do not censor your words; write down the first words that come to mind.
You often have to go through wild ideas to get to the actionable good ideas (David Kelley, d.school).
The bigger and more graphic your mind map, the better it is for generating lots of ideas.
Anchor problems are a class of problems that, like a physical anchor, hold you in one place and prevent motion.
In good life design, it is important to notice when you are stuck with an anchor problem.
Being anchored to a single, idealized solution keeps you stuck in an immovable situation.
If a solution feels 'too hard,' you will not do it—too hard doesn't work.
Getting unanchored requires reframing the goal to something achievable and prototyping a little.
Breaking a large, overwhelming project into smaller, manageable steps makes progress possible.
The problem is not that the task is impossible (a gravity problem); it is that you are anchored to a solution that can't work.
Reimagining a different result or intermediate steps along the way is the key to moving forward.
Anchoring yourself to a single solution—especially a bad one—leads to prolonged stuckness and failure.
There is a critical difference between your actual problem and your first idea of a solution to that problem.
When you anchor to a bad solution, the negative effects compound over time: depression, suffering in other areas of life, and social isolation from colleagues.
Adopting a design thinking mind-set, remembering your real problem, and exploring prototypes can help you get unstuck.
Applying curiosity and investigating alternatives before settling on an approach prevents premature commitment to a single path.
Framing an interesting question and talking to lots of people is a way to broaden your understanding of the problem before choosing a solution.
Reframing a problem from a large, nearly impossible goal to smaller, cheaper alternatives can unlock progress and enlist more supporters.
Prototyping—testing an idea in a low-stakes, incremental way—builds credibility and works the idea into existing culture before a full commitment is made.
Radical collaboration (forming joint teams, inviting others to co-own the idea) distributes the burden and creates institutional advocates beyond a single person.
A lasting institutional impact is possible without the 'cooler and bigger' solution, as long as the smaller path is pursued with persistence.

Repeated near-misses (e.g., dieting down a few pounds each year but never crossing the threshold) can cause a goal to quietly expire as external circumstances (kids growing up, bodies changing) shift beyond recovery.
Don't make a doable problem into an anchor problem by wedding yourself irretrievably to a solution that just isn't working.
Anchor problems keep us stuck because we can only see one solution—the one we already have that doesn't work.
Anchor problems are really about the fear that, no matter what else we try, that won't work either, and then we'll have to admit we're permanently stuck.
It is often more comfortable to hold on to a familiar, failed approach than to risk a worse failure by attempting big changes.
Change is always uncertain, and there is no guarantee of success, no matter how hard you try.
The way forward is to reduce the risk (and the fear) of failure by designing a series of small prototypes to test the waters.
Prototypes are supposed to fail—they teach you something about the future, lower anxiety, and provide data about the potential of the change.
A core design-thinking principle is to 'fail fast and fail forward' into your next step.
Anchor problems differ from gravity problems: an anchor problem is a real, actionable problem that seems insurmountable only because we've been stuck on it too long or too often.
Gravity problems are not actually problems; they are circumstances you can do nothing to change, and the only response is acceptance and redirection.
If a problem isn't actionable, then it's not solvable; designers know better than to go up against the laws of nature or the marketplace.
The goal of life design is to generate lots of ideas and lots of options so you can build prototypes of your life and test them out.
Mind mapping from your Good Time Journal helps surface engagement, energy, and flow experiences as a foundation for inventing new life alternatives.
The purpose of the mind-mapping exercise is to defer judgment and quiet your internal problem-finding critic, not to produce a specific result.
By imagining how to combine elements creatively into surprising roles or jobs, you shift from problem-solving (what do I do next?) into design thinking (what can I imagine?).
Working with a designer's mind-set means letting your mind go all over the place and ideating without judgment.
The next major task after mind mapping is to innovate three real alternative lives, called Odyssey Plans.
If the exercise felt silly, it likely means you did not successfully defer judgment; you can revisit your work or try again in a few days.

exercises.title: Good Time Journal
exercises.purpose: To help you identify which activities in your daily life genuinely engage and energize you versus those that drain you, so you can recognize where you are stuck.
steps: Track your daily activities and note which ones engage and energize you and which ones do not.
Review the journal to identify patterns of activities that leave you feeling like a 'small, unimportant cog' versus activities that make you feel you are leaving a mark.
materials: A journal or notebook for tracking daily activities
exercises.source_quote: after doing his Good Time Journal, he realized he was spending the majority of his days in activities that neither engaged nor energized him

exercises.title: Dysfunctional Belief Reframe
exercises.purpose: To challenge the limiting belief that you are stuck and replace it with a designer's mindset that you can always generate many ideas.
steps: Identify your dysfunctional belief (e.g., 'I'm stuck.').
Reframe it into a designer-oriented statement (e.g., 'I'm never stuck, because I can always generate a lot of ideas.').
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: I'm stuck.
Reframe: I'm never stuck, because I can always generate a lot of ideas.

exercises.title: Dysfunctional Belief / Reframe
exercises.purpose: To help the reader identify the limiting belief that there is only one correct path or idea and consciously replace it with a more expansive, exploratory mindset.
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'I have to find the one right idea.'
Reframe it: 'I need a lot of ideas so that I can explore any number of possibilities for my future.'
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: I have to find the one right idea.
Reframe: I need a lot of ideas so that I can explore any number of possibilities for my future.

exercises.title: Ideate This
exercises.purpose: To get the reader out of the box of realism and into a wide, open exploration of 'what I might want,' generating a large quantity of wild and crazy ideas to break free from the pressure of finding a single perfect answer.
steps: Accept the problem and get stuck.
Get over it and shift into ideation mode.
Get out of the box of being realistic.
Venture into the wide world of 'what I might want.'
Embrace being stuck as a starting point.
Generate lots of ideas and possibilities—wild ideas, crazy ideas—more than you ever thought possible.
exercises.source_quote: We're going to ask you to get out of the box of being realistic and venture into the wide world of "what I might want." It's time to embrace being stuck.

exercises.title: How Many Lifetimes Are in You?
exercises.purpose: To shift the reader away from the belief that there is only one 'right' life design and toward the liberating recognition that multiple great lives are possible within them.
steps: Ask yourself: 'How many lifetimes' worth of living are there in you?'
Reflect on your answer (the authors report an average of 3.4 among their students).
Accept the idea that there are multiple great designs for your life, even though you will only get to live one, and let that recognition feel liberating.
exercises.source_quote: When we ask our students, "How many lifetimes' worth of living are there in you?," the average answer is 3.4.

exercises.title: Mind Mapping
exercises.purpose: To generate a wide range of ideas by using free association of words, helping you overcome the bias toward the obvious and regain creative confidence when you are stuck.
steps: Use simple free association of words, one after another, to open up the idea space.
Come up with new solutions by following the chain of associated words.
exercises.source_quote: Mind mapping works by using simple free association of words, one after another, to open up the idea space and come up with new solutions.

exercises.title: Mind Mapping
exercises.purpose: To generate a large volume of ideas and unexpected connections by using a fast, visual free-association process that bypasses the inner logical/verbal censor, ultimately producing novel concepts by mashing together peripheral associations.
steps: Pick a topic (for example, a positive experience identified in a Good Time Journal) and write it in the center of a page, drawing a circle around it.
Write down five or six things related to that central idea, being rigorous in writing down the first words that come to mind.
For each word in the second ring, draw three or four lines and free-associate new words related to that specific word (not the central topic).
Repeat the branching process until you have at least three or four rings of word associations.
Keep the entire process to three to five minutes so you work fast and bypass your inner censor.
Look at the completed map and highlight a few words that seem interesting or jump out at you, choosing from the very outer layer or perimeter.
Mash the highlighted random words together into a few new concepts.
exercises.source_quote:
The mind-mapping process has three steps:
1. Picking a topic
2. Making the mind map

3. Making secondary connections and creating concepts (mashing it
all up)

exercises.title: Big-Paper Mind Map for Idea Generation
exercises.purpose: To break free from feeling stuck by rapidly generating a wide range of ideas—wild and practical alike—by visually mapping components of your situation on a large surface, using your current circumstances as a springboard.
steps: Identify the individual components of your situation (e.g., interests, skills, locations, activities) and list them.
Mash the individual components together into possible new ideas or combinations.
Write down the first words that come to mind; do not censor yourself.
Do the exercise fast to avoid self-editing.
Create the mind map on a big piece of paper, making it as graphic and as big as possible.
Use a giant piece of butcher paper or a large white board.
Have big ideas; go through the wild ideas to reach the actionable good ideas.
Look for ways your current job or situation can serve as a springboard to what's next.
materials: A giant piece of butcher paper or a large white board
Markers or pens for writing and drawing
exercises.source_quote: Also, you should create your mind map on a big piece of paper. You are looking for lots of ideas—so make your map as graphic and as big as possible. Go out and get a giant piece of butcher paper or a large white board, and have big ideas.

exercises.title: Reframe and Prototype to Get Unanchored
exercises.purpose: To help a person break free from being stuck on an overwhelming problem by redefining the goal to something achievable and breaking the work into smaller, doable steps.
steps: Reframe the goal so it is smaller and more realistic (e.g., aim for just a workbench and inside storage for bikes and camping gear rather than a perfect full garage layout).
Consider an alternative reframe that accepts a partial external solution (e.g., keep one small storage unit for life and rent back garage space for about a hundred dollars a month).

Be mindful of process and break the work into smaller projects: (a) give away old books and music, (b) reduce to only four bikes, (c) clear the floor of boxes, (d) clear the workbench of old project detritus.
Get rid of the image of the perfect end-state and reimagine a different result or steps along the way.
exercises.source_quote: The only way Dave can get unanchored from this immovable situation is to reframe his solution and prototype a little.

exercises.title: Reframe and Prototype to Get Unstuck from an Anchor Problem
exercises.purpose: To break free from an anchor problem by shifting from a single fixed solution to an open exploration, then testing small, low-risk versions of alternative approaches to reduce fear and gather data.
steps: Recognize that your current single solution, though not impossible, is taking too long to achieve and has a low chance of success.

Reframe the challenge as an exploration of possibilities instead of trying to solve the huge problem in one miraculous leap (e.g., change 'Take the Grand Canyon Mule Ride' to 'See the Grand Canyon Top to Bottom').
Identify multiple alternative ways to accomplish the broader goal (e.g., by helicopter, by river, by foot).
Decide to try a series of small, safe prototypes of the change you'd like to see happen (e.g., take some test hikes).
Treat prototype failures as expected and informative; use the data they provide to 'fail fast and fail forward' into your next step.
exercises.source_quote: When you're stuck with an anchor problem, try reframing the challenge as an exploration of possibilities (instead of trying to solve your huge problem in one miraculous leap), then decide to try a series of small, safe prototypes of the change you'd like to see happen.

exercises.title: Mind Mapping with Your Good Time Journal (Engagement, Energy, Flow)
exercises.purpose: To surface and expand on your most engaging, energizing, and flow-inducing experiences so you have rich material for generating new life options.
steps: If you haven't completed your Good Time Journal from the previous chapter, go back and do it now.

Mind Map 1 – Engagement: From your Good Time Journal, pick one area of greatest interest or an activity during which you were really engaged (e.g., balancing the budget or pitching a new idea). Place it at the center of a mind map and generate connected words and concepts, extending at least three or four layers with at least a dozen or more elements in the outermost ring.

Mind Map 2 – Energy: From your Good Time Journal, pick something you've identified as really energizing you in your work and life (e.g., art class, giving feedback to colleagues, health-care access, keeping things running right). Mind-map this out with the same depth and breadth.

Mind Map 3 – Flow: From your Good Time Journal, pick one experience when you were in a state of flow. Put the experience itself at the center of a mind map and complete your mapping of that experience (e.g., speaking in front of a large audience or brainstorming creative ideas).
materials: Completed Good Time Journal (from the previous chapter)
Large sheets of paper for each mind map
Pens or markers in multiple colors
exercises.source_quote: We are going to do three different mind maps, each one extending out at least three or four layers, and with at least a dozen or more elements in the outermost ring.

exercises.title: Invent a Life Alternative from Your Mind Maps
exercises.purpose: To combine disparate elements from your mind maps into a fun, interesting, and helpful (though not necessarily practical) life alternative, then name and sketch it to make the idea concrete.
steps: Look at the outer ring of one of your mind maps and pick three disparate items that catch your eye intuitively—they should literally 'jump out' at you.

Combine those three items into a possible job description that would be fun and interesting to you and would be helpful to someone else. It need not be practical or appeal to lots of people or employers.
Name your role and draw a napkin sketch of it—a quick visual drawing of what it is.
Repeat this process for each of the three mind maps (Engagement, Energy, and Flow) to generate three life alternatives.
materials: The three completed mind maps
Paper for the napkin sketch
Pen or pencil for drawing
exercises.source_quote: Now that you've done these three mind maps, we're going to invent an interesting, though not necessarily practical, life alternative from each.

exercises.title: Mind Mapping
exercises.purpose: To get your mind going all over the place and ideating without judgment, moving you out of problem-solving mode and into a designer's mind-set by exploring activities where you felt engaged, energized, and in flow.
steps: Review your Good Time Journal and note activities in which you were engaged, energized, and in flow.
Choose an activity that you were engaged in, an activity that you felt highly energized from, and something you did that brought you into flow, and create three mind maps—one for each.
Look at the outer ring of each mind map, pick three things that jump out at you, and create a job description from them.
Create a role for each job description, and draw a napkin sketch.
Do this exercise three times—once for each of your mind maps—making sure that the three versions are different from one another.
materials: Good Time Journal
Paper for mind maps and napkin sketches
Writing and drawing supplies
exercises.source_quote: 1. Review your Good Time Journal and note activities in which you were engaged, energized, and in flow.

key_ideas: You will live many different lives in this single lifetime; the life you are currently living is just one of many.
Life design gives you 'endless mulligans'—you can do it over at any point, at any time, and 'correction shots' are always allowed.
A common mistake is believing you need one perfect plan or blueprint for your life, as if life were paint-by-numbers.
Life is more like an abstract painting, open to multiple interpretations, rather than a single correct path.
We all contain enough energy, talents, and interests to live many different types of lives, all of which can be authentic, interesting, and productive.
Asking which life is 'best' is a silly question, like asking whether it is better to have hands or feet.
The story of Chung illustrates the paralysis that comes from believing there is one right choice and that picking wrong means settling for a 'second choice' life.
There is no single 'best' path in life; there are multiple great and substantially different possibilities available to you.

The dysfunctional belief that you must figure out your best possible life, make a plan, and execute it should be reframed as: there are multiple great lives within you, and you get to choose which one to build your way forward to next.
Designing your 'lives' (plural) is one of the most powerful ways to design your life.
Every person has at least three viable and substantially different possibilities within them.
When you stop trying to 'get it right' and start designing your way forward, unexpected and better paths can emerge.
Having life-design tools and confidence in multiple happy paths helps you navigate post-college (or post-transition) stress and even help others do the same.
You should develop three Odyssey Plans—alternative life plans—in parallel rather than committing to a single path.
Research from the Stanford Graduate School of Education shows that starting with multiple ideas in parallel produces more and better final solutions than iterating on a single idea serially.
Each Odyssey Plan is a 'Plan A'—it is really you and really possible—not a ranked hierarchy of A, B, C.
Odyssey Plans are sketches of possibilities meant to animate your imagination and help you choose a direction to start prototyping.
Choosing among the alternatives (based on resources, coherence, confidence, and preference) is a separate step addressed later; first you must develop the alternatives.
Life is an odyssey—an adventurous journey into the future with hopes, goals, helpers, unknowns, and serendipities unfolding over time.
Life can be understood as an adventure or quest, like the story of Odysseus.
Five years is the ideal planning horizon: two years is too short and seven is too long.
Most people's lives are actually lived as a series of two-to-four-year seasons strung together.
Creating three truly different alternative life plans (not variations on a theme) gives real choices and stretches creative muscles.
The three plans should be genuinely distinct alternatives, not two versions of the same idea.

You can generate multiple life alternatives by working through three distinct prompts: Life One (what you'd do), Life Two (what you'd do if Life One disappeared), and Life Three (what you'd do if money or image were no object).
Life Three is specifically the thing you'd do if you knew you could make a decent living at it and no one would laugh at you or think less of you for doing it.
The process should not be overthought; the authors urge readers to 'really do it' because it is an exercise that will change your life.

Odyssey Planning involves creating three detailed alternative versions of the next five years of your life, each with a visual timeline, a six-word headline title, exploratory questions, and a feasibility dashboard.
A good designer asks questions to test assumptions and reveal new insights, and each potential timeline should investigate different possibilities to learn about yourself and the world.
The dashboard for each alternative includes gauging whether you have the objective resources—time, money, skill, contacts—needed to pull off the plan.
Odyssey Plans help define important things still to do in your life and help you remember dreams you may have forgotten.
Each alternative plan should be evaluated on Likability, Confidence, and Coherence.
When designing plans, consider geography, experience/learning, impacts/results, and what life will look like in a particular role, industry, or company.
Keep in mind things other than career and money when designing your alternative lives.
Make at least one of your Odyssey Plans a little bit wild or farfetched.
You can create different alternative plans for different areas of life: career, love, health, or play, or combine these elements.
The only wrong way to do Odyssey Plans is to not do them at all.
Each plan example includes a six-word headline, a four-gauge dashboard, and three questions the plan is asking.
There isn't a single right answer to what's next for you; having three versions of yourself helps you realize this.

When evaluating your Odyssey Plan alternatives, consider which rates high on resources, likability, confidence, and coherence, and which gives you a 'jazzy, feel-good, light-my-fire' feeling versus which feels draining.
The life design process is most effective in a group of three to six people who both do the work and support each other.
When sharing your plans, listeners should receive, reflect, and amplify—not critique, review, or advise.
Using 'Tell me more about…' as a question prompt keeps the inquiry supportive rather than evaluative.
If you cannot find a group, you can video yourself presenting your Odyssey Plans as an alternative.
Life design is about generating options, not finding a single definitive answer.
You are designing what's next, not the rest of your life.
Every possible version of you holds unknowns and compromises, each with identifiable and unintended consequences.
The goal is to embrace and explore questions and be curious about possibilities rather than seeking answers.
There are multiple great lives within you; you are legion.
You get to choose which prototype to start working on next.

exercises.title: Odyssey Plans
exercises.purpose: To break the belief that there is one 'best' life to figure out by having you imagine and write up three substantially different, viable versions of your next five years, revealing the multiple great lives within you.
steps: Imagine three different versions of the next five years of your life.
Ensure the three versions are viable and substantially different from one another.
Write up each of the three versions.
materials: Paper or notebook for writing up the three versions
exercises.source_quote: We're going to ask you to imagine and write up three different versions of the next five years of your life. We call these Odyssey Plans.

exercises.title: Develop Three Odyssey Plans
exercises.purpose: To ideate multiple variations of your life path in parallel so you can choose creatively and generatively, avoiding premature commitment to a single plan and staying open to novel possibilities.
steps: Come up with three different plans (Odyssey Plans) for your life, even if you already have a preferred or committed plan in mind.
Treat each Odyssey Plan as a 'Plan A'—it is really you and really possible—rather than ranking them as a good, okay, or fallback option.
Develop each plan as a sketch of a possibility that can animate your imagination and help you see which wayfinding direction you might take to start prototyping and living into next.
Do not worry yet about choosing which alternative life to live; focus on developing the alternatives first.
exercises.source_quote: you still need to develop three Odyssey Plan alternatives. Really. Some of the people who've gotten the most out of this exercise are the ones who entered into it already having all the answers to their One True Plan in place.

exercises.title: Create Three Very Different Five-Year Life Plans
exercises.purpose: To imagine multiple, genuinely distinct ways to launch the next chapter of your life's journey, giving yourself real choices and stretching your creative thinking beyond the obvious answer.
steps: Decide on a five-year timeframe for your plans (not two, not seven).
Create three very different alternative versions of your life for the next five years. They must be truly different alternatives, not variations on a theme.
Life One – That Thing You Do: Center your first plan on what you've already got in mind—either your current life expanded forward or that hot idea you've been nursing for some time.

Life Two – That Thing You'd Do If Thing One Were Suddenly Gone: Imagine your Life One idea is suddenly over or no longer an option. Force your imagination to believe you have to make a living doing something other than Life One. Decide what you would do.
Life Three: (The chapter text provided does not include the description of Life Three.)
exercises.source_quote: We want you to create three very different plans for the next five years of your life.

exercises.title: The Three Lives Exercise
exercises.purpose: To help a person who is stuck on a single life idea generate at least three distinct alternative life directions by working through three structured prompts.
steps: Identify your Life One: the thing you are currently doing or planning to do (e.g., 'I want to go into management consulting').
Identify your Life Two: imagine that Life One has completely disappeared (e.g., 'consulting just died') and ask yourself what you would do instead.
Identify your Life Three: imagine that you could make a decent living at it and that no one would laugh at you or think less of you for doing it, then ask yourself what you would do.
If you cannot come up with three ideas quickly, use the structured approach of Life One, Life Two, and Life Three to prompt yourself until you generate more than enough ideas.
Do not get stuck or overthink it; really do the exercise.
exercises.source_quote: If you can't come up with three ideas quickly, just try this approach to your life one, life two, and life three, and you'll probably find yourself getting more than enough ideas.

exercises.title: Odyssey Planning 101
exercises.purpose: To create three detailed, alternative five-year life plans that allow you to explore different possibilities, test assumptions, and learn about yourself and the world.
steps: Create three alternative versions of the next five years of your life.
For each version, build a visual/graphical timeline that includes personal and noncareer events (e.g., marriage, training for the CrossFit Games, learning to bend spoons with your mind).
Give each option a title in the form of a six-word headline describing the essence of that alternative.
Write two or three questions that this alternative is asking—things you will want to test and explore in each version of your life.
Build a dashboard where you can gauge feasibility, starting with Resources: ask whether you have the objective resources—time, money, skill, contacts—you need to pull off your plan.
exercises.source_quote: Create three alternative versions of the next five years of your life. Each one must include:

exercises.title: Create Three Odyssey Plans (Alternative Five-Year Lives)
exercises.purpose: To define important things still to do in your life, remember forgotten dreams, and explore multiple possible directions for the next five years by designing three distinct alternative plans.
steps: Generate three very different five-year alternative plans for your life, each a little more risky and innovative than the last.

For each plan, consider: geography (where you will live), what experience/learning you will gain, the impacts/results of choosing that alternative, and what life will look like (particular role, industry, or company).
Keep in mind things other than career and money when shaping each plan.

Make at least one of the plans a little bit wild—write down your most farfetched and crazy idea (e.g., living off the grid, trying to make it in Hollywood, extreme sports, hunting down a lost family member).
Optionally create different alternative plans for different areas of life (career, love, health, play) or combine these elements.

Evaluate each plan on Likability (are you hot, cold, or warm about it?), Confidence (are you feeling full of confidence or uncertain?), and Coherence (does the plan make sense within itself and is it consistent with you, your Workview, and your Lifeview?).
Give each plan a six-word headline describing it.
Create a four-gauge dashboard for each plan.
Identify the three questions each particular alternative plan is asking.
exercises.source_quote: For all of us, Odyssey Plans can define important things still to do in our lives, and help us remember dreams we may have forgotten.

exercises.title: Mind Map of Design Considerations
exercises.purpose: To unblock yourself when you feel stuck generating Odyssey Plans by visually exploring the various design considerations as a springboard for forming your alternative lives.
steps: Identify a design consideration from the list (geography, experience/learning, impacts/results, what life will look like, or other elements beyond career and money).
Make a mind map out of that design consideration, branching out ideas and possibilities.
Use the mind map as a springboard for forming your alternative lives for the next five years.
Don't overthink the exercise, and don't skip it.
exercises.source_quote: If you find yourself stuck, try making a mind map out of any of the design considerations listed above. Don't overthink this exercise, and don't skip it.

exercises.title: Odyssey Plan Exercise
exercises.purpose: To generate three distinct alternative five-year life plans so you can see that there is no single right path and to identify which version of you feels most energizing and coherent.
steps: Complete three alternative five-year plans of your own, one on each of the three worksheets provided (or downloadable at www.designingyour.life).

For each alternative, consider questions such as whether your skills translate, whether the idea is good enough, whether you can raise funding, whether you're ready for the risk, whether it will be meaningful, and whether it will be profitable.
Evaluate which alternative rates high on resources, likability, confidence, and coherence.
Identify which version of you gives you a 'jazzy, feel-good, light-my-fire' feeling and which version feels draining.
materials: Three Odyssey Plan worksheets (included in the book or downloadable at www.designingyour.life)
exercises.source_quote: Now complete three alternative five-year plans of your own, one on each of the three worksheets here or downloadable at www.designingyour.life.

exercises.title: Sharing the Three Versions of You
exercises.purpose: To present your Odyssey Plan alternatives aloud to a supportive group so you can receive feedback, ideas, and questions that deepen your understanding of each path without receiving unwanted critique or advice.
steps: Find two to five people who are 'there for you' and will show up for an evening dedicated to helping you design your life, or who are willing to read this chapter.
Set ground rules with your listeners: tell them not to critique, review, or advise; ask them to receive, reflect, and amplify.
Present your three Odyssey Plan alternatives aloud to the group.
When it is time for questions, guide listeners to use 'Tell me more about…' as their approach to keep the inquiry supportive.
If you cannot find a group, video yourself presenting your Odyssey Plans as an alternative.
materials: A group of two to five supportive people (or a video camera if presenting alone)
exercises.source_quote: The best way to interact with your alternatives is to share them aloud with a group of friends—ideally, with your Life Design Team (see chapter 11 for more on team and community) or the group you are reading this book with, as we suggested in the introduction.

exercises.title: Self-Observation and Jotting
exercises.purpose: To step outside your own narrative and notice what you want to say to yourself, generating raw material for life design.
steps: Watch and listen to yourself as though you weren't the author.
See what you have to say to yourself.
Jot down your ideas.

Paper or notebook to jot down ideas

steps: Create three alternative five-year plans, using the worksheet provided.
Give each alternative a descriptive six-word title, and write down three questions that arise out of each version of you.
Complete each gauge on the dashboard—ranking each alternative for resources, likability, confidence, and coherence.

key_ideas: Prototyping means trying out possibilities without committing to them prematurely—getting real experience in 'water up to your knees, not over your head.'
It is bad advice to simply 'jump in and just commit to something' when you have no clear direction, because you risk overcommitting to the wrong thing.
You can begin prototyping even without a specific goal, as long as you identify a broad area of interest to explore.
Actively researching and keeping your eye out for low-commitment opportunities is a practical way to start testing possibilities.
When evaluating a potential prototype, look for low time demands and no long-term obligation (e.g., a few hours a week, no binding commitment after a short course).
The concept of an 'encore career'—a meaningful next phase after a long professional career—can be discovered through prototyping rather than through a single grand plan.
You do not need a specific mission or plan to begin; you can design your way forward through small, illustrative experiences.
Prototyping means doing small experiments—trying things out in low-stakes, limited ways—to learn what you are drawn to.
The path to a passion or encore career is rarely a straight line; it is built step by step through successive prototypes.
Thinking like a designer means crafting a series of small involvements that each teach you something and narrow your focus.
Exploration is valid: you can engage part-time or temporarily while still searching, without committing fully.
Each prototype (e.g., a short course, a part-time role, a board seat) provides real-world data that a plan alone cannot.
"Building is thinking" — prototyping is a form of thinking, not just making.
When designing your life, you lack reliable data about your future, so traditional cause-and-effect thinking won't work.
Prototyping is about asking good questions, outing hidden biases and assumptions, iterating rapidly, and creating momentum for a path you'd like to try out.
Prototypes are NOT about checking whether your solution is right, nor about creating a representation of a completed design.
Designers make lots of prototypes — never just one.
Good prototypes isolate one aspect of a problem and design an experience that lets you 'try out' a potentially interesting future.
Hands-on experience (doing the work, meeting people, exploring options) is what leads to discovery, not just reading, thinking, or journaling.
The bias-to-action mind-set combined with 'building is thinking' produces a lot of building and thinking.
Prototyping lets you imagine your future experientially, as if you are already living it, giving you a feel for a new career path even for just an hour or a day.
Prototypes help involve others early, build a community around your journey, and frequently turn into unexpected opportunities through serendipity.
Prototypes allow you to try and fail rapidly without overinvesting in a path before you have any data.
The best way to start prototyping is to keep the first few prototypes very low-resolution and very simple, isolating one variable to answer one question.
A prototype is not a thought experiment; it must involve a physical experience in the real world to generate the data needed for good decisions.
Prototyping is about building empathy and understanding through collaboration with others, revealing their life designs and giving you ideas for your own.
The purposes of prototyping are to ask good questions, create experiences, reveal assumptions, fail fast, fail forward, sneak up on the future, and build empathy.
Not prototyping is a bad and sometimes very costly idea, as illustrated by Elise's story of going all-in on a dream business without testing it first.
Prototyping a life idea before fully committing saves time, money, and emotional pain, even when you feel rushed.
The simplest and easiest form of prototyping is a conversation with someone who is living the life you are contemplating.
You must learn the full, unglamorous reality of a role—what the person loves, hates, and what their ordinary days look like—not just the attractive surface.
Most people fail not for lack of talent but for lack of imagination about what a role actually entails day to day.
A successful outcome (like a profitable café) does not mean the role is the right fit; you may be great at one aspect and miserable in another.
A Life Design Interview is not a job interview; it is a conversation focused on getting the story of the person you are with.
The mindset of a job interview is critique and judgment, which is the opposite of the curiosity and personal connection a Life Design Interview requires.
If you find yourself answering questions or talking about yourself during a Life Design Interview, you must stop and flip the conversation back to the other person's story.
When requesting a meeting, you should identify people currently doing work you find interesting and whose stories you want to hear, framing it as a shared interest rather than a job inquiry.
A 'no' to a meeting request is actually a kind act, as it frees you to find someone who can genuinely be helpful.
The term 'interview' should be avoided when requesting the meeting because it triggers job-interview assumptions in the other person.
Prototype conversations are informative, but you also need to actually experience what a future life would be like, not just hear about it.
Prototype experiences allow you to learn through a direct encounter with a possible future version of yourself.
Forms of prototype experiences include shadowing a professional, a short unpaid exploratory project, an internship, or a hands-on task in the field.
After conducting a number of prototype conversations, you are in a better position to make a bigger request such as shadowing someone at work.
Hands-on prototype experiences—where you actually do the work rather than watch or listen—are harder to arrange but essential for discovering how something fits you.
You should 'test drive' a job or life change before committing, just as you would test-drive a car before buying it.
Conceiving hands-on prototype experiences is real design work that requires generating many ideas.
Design brainstorming is a collaborative technique for finding lots of ideas, and it is the appropriate tool for generating prototype experience options.
Referrals and networking significantly improve your ability to access prototype opportunities.

Brainstorming, as described by Alex Osborn in 1953's Applied Imagination, relies on two rules: generating a large quantity of ideas without concern for quality, and deferring judgment so participants do not censor ideas.
The goal of life design brainstorming is to generate ideas that can be prototyped and tried in the real world.
Good brainstormers are compared to improvisational jazz musicians: they focus on a topic but also let go, stay in-the-moment, and improvise truly original ideas.
Life design brainstorming follows a structured four-step approach and requires a small group of volunteers (no fewer than three, rarely more than six).
Before brainstorming, you should revisit your Odyssey Plans to identify which version was coherent, likable, and exciting, and generate specific questions you want answered through prototyping.
Open-ended brainstorming questions produce more interesting and voluminous results than closed ones.
The phrase 'How many ways can we think of to…' is a reliable framing that avoids limiting potential output.
Including a solution in the brainstorming question (e.g., 'ten new ways to make a ladder') narrows the solution space and caps the number of ideas.
Focusing on the function of a solution rather than the solution itself (e.g., 'give a person access to inventory in high places') opens up more creative answers.
Questions framed too broadly (e.g., 'make Bob happy') fail because key terms are ambiguous and lack context, producing ideas that are neither prototypable nor satisfying.
The most common reason a brainstorm 'didn't work' is a poorly framed question—either assuming a solution or being too vague for traction.
Participants need a transitional activity to shift from an analytical/critical mindset to a synthesizing/nonjudgmental creative state before brainstorming.
Warming up is a mind-body problem that takes practice, and a good facilitator takes the lead to ensure everyone is ready.
Brainstorming sessions must be facilitated to maintain energy, structure, and safety.
Go for quantity over quality to keep the group bubbling with ideas and positive energy.
Deferring judgment creates a safe space where fear of being judged does not shut down creativity.
Building off the ideas of others leverages the collective creativity of the group, like a jazz quartet riffing on each other's musical ideas.
Encouraging wild ideas breaks the group out of typical thinking; the ideas that follow tend to be more innovative and contain the seeds of the most useful prototypes.
Participants should write down their own ideas on personal notepads so the group is not constrained by the facilitator's recording speed and no idea is lost.
Naming and framing the outcomes immediately after a brainstorm is critical; otherwise the freshness of the ideas and their interconnections get lost.
Tactile, playful materials like Play-Doh can shift adults into a more creative, childlike state during brainstorming.
Ideas from a brainstorm should be counted so participants can see tangible output (e.g., 'We had 141 ideas').
Grouping similar ideas into named categories and framing them against the original focal question gives structure to the brainstorm.
Voting should be done silently (e.g., with colored dots) so participants don't influence one another.
Creative voting categories (e.g., 'The dark horse,' 'If we could ignore the laws of physics…') help surface different kinds of ideas.
The end goal of the four-step process is to narrow down to a prioritized list of prototypes to build first.
A wild, seemingly impossible idea can often be backed off just enough to become a great, actionable idea.
Brainstorming generates energy and momentum and can be revisited whenever new ideas, community support, or fun are needed.
Combining an Odyssey Plan presentation gathering with a prototype brainstorm session lets collaborators contribute directly to your life design.
Prototypes are built by actively seeking out Life Design Interviews and experiences.
This is step 5 in a broader prototyping process.

exercises.title: Prototyping: Test-Drive a Possibility in Low-Commitment Water
exercises.purpose: To help a reader who feels stuck without a clear next direction begin exploring options safely, gaining real experience without the risk of overcommitting to the wrong path.
steps: Recognize that you need to try things out first without committing yourself to them prematurely; aim for 'water up to your knees, not over your head.'
Identify a broad area of interest, even if you do not yet have a specific goal (e.g., Clara chose 'helping women' based on her background as a feminist and former IBM salesperson).
Actively research approaches within that area of interest and keep your eye out for things you could try.
When a potential opportunity arises (e.g., a talk, a class, a workshop), introduce yourself, ask sharp questions, and learn what is involved.

Evaluate the opportunity for low commitment: check the time required (e.g., 'only a few hours a week') and whether there is any binding obligation after completion (e.g., 'no obligation' after a certification test).
Sign up and participate in the low-commitment experience to gain real, hands-on experience with the possibility.
exercises.source_quote: She wanted to test-drive some possibilities, get some real experience, but do it in water up to her knees, not over her head.

exercises.title: Dysfunctional Belief / Reframe
exercises.purpose: To identify a limiting belief about planning and replace it with a prototyping-oriented mindset that encourages action over exhaustive research.
steps: Identify your dysfunctional belief about planning (e.g., 'If I comprehensively research the best data for all aspects of my plan, I'll be fine.').
Reframe it into a prototyping-oriented statement (e.g., 'I should build prototypes to explore questions about my alternatives.').
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: If I comprehensively research the best data for all aspects of my plan, I'll be fine.
Reframe: I should build prototypes to explore questions about my alternatives.

exercises.title: Design a Prototype to Ask a Question
exercises.purpose: To create a low-stakes, hands-on experience that isolates one aspect of a life question and generates data about a potentially interesting future.
steps: Identify a question about an alternative future you are interested in.
Isolate one aspect of that problem or question.
Design an experience that allows you to 'try out' some version of that potentially interesting future.
Build the prototype (a physical object, a conversation, a short experience, a policy sketch, etc.).
Use the prototype to get data and surface hidden biases or assumptions.
Iterate rapidly based on what you learn; make more prototypes rather than settling on one.
exercises.source_quote: Prototypes should be designed to ask a question and get some data about something that you're interested in. Good prototypes isolate one aspect of a problem and design an experience that allows you to "try out" some version of a potentially interesting future.

exercises.title: Low-Resolution Prototyping Practice
exercises.purpose: To generate real-world data about a desired life direction by designing a simple, physical experience that isolates one variable, allowing you to fail fast and iterate without overinvesting.
steps: Identify one specific question you want to answer about a potential life direction.
Design a prototype that isolates that single variable and is very low-resolution and very simple.
Use what you already have available or can ask for; do not overinvest in materials or time.
Ensure the prototype involves a physical experience in the real world, not merely a thought experiment.
Carry out the prototype and engage with the real world to gather data.
Be prepared to iterate quickly based on what you learn.
Involve others in the process to build empathy, spark conversation, and open the door to unexpected opportunities.
exercises.source_quote: The best way to get started is to keep your first few prototypes very low-resolution and very simple. You want to isolate one variable and design a prototype to answer that one question. Use what you have available or can ask for, and be prepared to iterate quickly. And remember that a prototype is not a thought experiment; it must involve a physical experience in the world.

exercises.title: Life Design Interview
exercises.purpose: To prototype a life idea by sitting down with someone who is doing (or has expertise in) the role you are contemplating and extracting their full personal story, so you can honestly assess whether you can imagine yourself in that role for months and years.
steps: Identify a person who is either doing and living what you are contemplating, or who has real experience and expertise in an area about which you have questions.
Sit down with that person and ask for their personal story: how they got to be doing what they do, or how they acquired their expertise.
Ask what they love and hate about their job.
Ask what their typical days look like.
Reflect on whether you can imagine yourself doing that job—and loving it—for months and years on end.
Ask how they got there: their career path and the steps that led them to this point.
exercises.source_quote: A Life Design Interview is incredibly simple. It just means getting someone's story.

exercises.title: Life Design Interview
exercises.purpose: To build a personal connection and learn the story of someone whose work or path you find interesting, using curiosity rather than critique or self-promotion.
steps: Identify a person who is currently doing things you are interested in and whose story you want to hear.

Request a meeting by referencing a mutual connection, expressing genuine admiration for their work, and asking for thirty minutes at a time and place convenient to them, offering to buy them a cup of coffee.
During the conversation, focus entirely on getting the story of the person you are with rather than answering questions or talking about yourself.
If you find yourself slipping into answering questions or talking about yourself, stop and flip the conversation back to the other person's story.
Maintain a mindset of curiosity and personal connection, not critique or judgment.
exercises.source_quote: In fact, a Life Design Interview isn't an "interview" at all—it's really just a conversation.

exercises.title: Prototype Experiences (Shadowing / Hands-On Exploration)
exercises.purpose: To learn through a direct encounter with a possible future version of yourself by actually doing or observing the work, rather than relying solely on stories from prototype conversations.
steps: Identify people you met during your Life Design Interviewing (prototype conversations) whom you might be interested in observing or shadowing.
Ask to shadow a professional for a day (a 'Take a Friend to Work Day') or for a longer period.
Alternatively, create a one-week unpaid exploratory project in the area you want to explore.
Alternatively, pursue a three-month internship if you are ready for a larger commitment.
For hands-on experiences, conceive specific small-scale tasks you could actually perform (e.g., catering a few times, taking a short-term job bussing tables) rather than just watching or listening.
Make the request to the person or organization; be prepared to try a few times if necessary.
Reflect on what you learned from the direct experience.
exercises.source_quote: Prototype experiences allow us to learn through a direct encounter with a possible future version of us. This experiential version could involve spending a day shadowing a professional you'd like to be (Take a Friend to Work Day), or a one-week unpaid exploratory project that you create, or a three-month internship

exercises.title: Life Design Brainstorming Session
exercises.purpose: To generate a large quantity of prototypable life design ideas in a structured group setting, using Osborn's rules of quantity over quality and deferred judgment.
steps: Assemble a team of no fewer than three and rarely more than six people who have all volunteered to help.
Frame a good question for the brainstorming session (Step 1: Framing a Good Question).
Select a focal question or problem on which to brainstorm.
Spend a period of twenty minutes to an hour generating as many ideas as possible to solve the problem posed in the focal question.
Aim to come up with ideas that can be prototyped and tried in the real world.
exercises.source_quote: Life design brainstorming has four steps, and a very structured approach to coming up with lots of prototypable ideas. Typically, if you are the facilitator who brings the group together, you might have already framed the brainstorming topic. You want a team of no fewer than three and rarely more than six people who have all volunteered to help.

exercises.title: Framing a Brainstorming Question
exercises.purpose: To create a well-scoped, open-ended question that focuses the group's energy and maximizes the volume and creativity of ideas generated during a brainstorm.
steps: Formulate an open-ended question for the brainstorm session.
Use the phrase 'How many ways can we think of to…' to ensure the question does not limit potential output.

Check that the question does not accidentally include a specific solution; instead, focus on the function or need the solution addresses (e.g., 'give a person access to inventory in high places' rather than 'make a ladder').

Check that the question is not so broad it becomes meaningless; add context or constraints (e.g., specify 'my work' or 'my social life') so participants know where to start and can generate prototypable ideas.
Review the question against the four-step method before beginning the brainstorm to avoid the most common cause of failed sessions.
exercises.source_quote: When coming up with the question, the facilitator needs to be aware of some guidelines.

exercises.title: Warming Up (Step 2 of the Four-Step Brainstorming Method)
exercises.purpose: To help participants transition from a hectic, analytical/critical workday mindset into a state of relaxed, creative, nonjudgmental attention so they can brainstorm effectively.
steps: The facilitator takes the lead in guiding the group through a transitional activity.
Use a transitional activity designed to shift the group from an analytical/critical brain state to a synthesizing/nonjudgmental brain state.
Ensure everyone is warmed up and feeling ready before moving on to the next step of the brainstorm.
exercises.source_quote: People need a transition from their hectic, event-driven workday to a state of relaxed, creative attention if they are going to do a good job brainstorming.

exercises.title: Play-Doh Brainstorming Warm-Up
exercises.purpose: To get brainstormers into a high-energy, creative state by letting them play with a tactile material that 'turns adults into children again,' resulting in more and better ideas.
steps: Give every member of the brainstorming group a can of Play-Doh.
Let the participants play with the Play-Doh while they are brainstorming.
materials: Cans of Play-Doh (one per participant)
exercises.source_quote: give everyone in your brainstorming group a can of PlayDoh

exercises.title: Facilitated Brainstorming Session
exercises.purpose: To generate a high volume of creative, unfiltered ideas in a structured group setting where participants feel safe to contribute and build on one another's thinking.
steps: The facilitator sets up the room, ensuring there are pens and sticky notes or paper for every participant and that the space is quiet and comfortable.
The facilitator helps frame the question for the group.
The facilitator manages the warm-up activity.
Each participant uses their own pen and notepad to write down their ideas as they come.
The facilitator records everything that is said and manages the rules.
Apply Rule 1: Go for quantity, not quality.
Apply Rule 2: Defer judgment and do not censor ideas.
Apply Rule 3: Build off the ideas of others.
Apply Rule 4: Encourage wild ideas.
materials: Pens (one per participant)
Sticky notes or paper (for each participant)
Personal notepads (for each participant)

exercises.title: Brainstorm, Categorize, and Vote on Prototype Ideas
exercises.purpose: To transform a raw list of brainstormed ideas into a structured, prioritized set of prototype candidates by counting, grouping, naming, and voting on them.
steps: Count all the ideas generated in the brainstorm so you can state a total (e.g., 'We had 141 ideas').
Group similar ideas together by subject or category.
Give each unique category a descriptive (and often funny) name that captures the essence of that group of ideas.
Frame the results with reference to the original focal question.

Vote silently using colored dots, assigning votes to categories such as 'Most exciting,' 'The one we wish we could do if money were no object,' 'The dark horse—probably won't work, but if it did…,' 'Most likely to lead to a great life,' and 'If we could ignore the laws of physics…'.
Once voting is complete, discuss the selections.
Potentially regroup and reframe the ideas again.
Make decisions on what to prototype first and prioritize the list.

Summarize the outcome in a statement like: 'We had 141 ideas, we grouped those into six categories, and, based on our focal question, we selected eight killer ideas to prototype; then we prioritized the list, and our first prototype is…'
materials: Colored dots for silent voting
Paper or whiteboard for listing and grouping ideas

9.chapter_title: 7. How Not to Get a Job
key_ideas: The standard American model of job seeking (résumé, cover letter, job postings) has a success rate of less than 5 percent, yet 90 percent of job seekers rely on it.
The standard model is built on the mistaken assumption that your perfect job is out there waiting for you to find it.
52 percent of employers have admitted they respond to fewer than half of the candidates who apply.
Perfection does not play a role in life design; the pursuit of the 'perfect' job, résumé, or cover letter is counterproductive.
The standard model involves finding a listing, reading the description, deciding if it is 'perfect,' submitting a résumé and cover letter, and then waiting indefinitely.
The Internet is not the be-all and end-all for job searching.
The belief that great jobs can be found by searching the Internet is a dysfunctional belief that leads to frustration and demoralization.
Most dream jobs, exciting start-up positions, and roles at small companies are never publicly listed online.
Large companies typically post their most interesting jobs internally only, invisible to most job seekers.
Internet job hunting is extremely time-consuming (crafting cover letters, tailoring résumés, tracking dozens of applications) and yields mostly silence.
Using the Internet as your only job-finding method is described as 'nothing short of masochistic.'
Job descriptions on websites are typically not written by the hiring manager or someone who truly understands the job.
Job descriptions almost never capture what the job actually requires for success, because hiring managers are too busy to write them accurately.
Job descriptions typically contain three sections: generic attributes, specific skills, and a 'what makes the candidate special' section.
The generic attributes section (e.g., good communication, strong analytical skills, highly motivated) describes qualities of any good employee and tells you nothing specific about the job.
The specific skills section is based on the previous jobholder's experience and is historical; it does not account for how the role, software, or procedures will change in the near future.

The 'what makes the candidate special' section often inadvertently reveals the truth about the job: phrases like 'not for the faint of heart' signal a bad job, and 'superheroes' signals an impossible workload.
Job descriptions are frequently written by overworked HR staff or office managers, which explains their generic and contradictory nature.
The very specific knowledge and software skills listed in a job description may become irrelevant within months as the company evolves.

The 'wishful thinking' qualifier: job descriptions use flattering words (insightful, persuasive, elegant, inspiring) that every candidate believes applies to them, making them useless for differentiating candidates.
These generic words are taken directly from major corporate job websites and are unlikely to attract only the best-qualified candidates.
To get your résumé discovered in a company's HR database, you must 'fit in' by using the same words the company uses in the job description before you try to 'stand out.'
Most mid-to-large companies scan résumés into a talent management database; the hiring manager discovers candidates via keyword search, and the most common keywords come from the job description.
Specific required skills are important but often not a deal-breaker; the descriptions are written from the point of view of the current job, not the future.
In the screening phase, focus exclusively on the skills match; mentioning unrelated talents makes you appear unfocused, uninterested, or like a bad listener.
The softball analogy: if the manager needs a pitcher, talk only about pitching—not catching, fielding, or baseball trivia.
Trying to 'stand out' at the beginning of the hiring process will get you ejected from the candidate pool.
Using the exact keywords from a job posting in your résumé improves your chance of being discovered in a keyword search.
Be generous with self-description on your résumé; modesty is not the time.
Focus your résumé on what you can do for the company, not on why the job works for you.
Do not appear to be a generalist or multidisciplinary person on your résumé or in the first interview.
The 'Super-Job Description Syndrome' means companies often post unrealistic qualifications that no candidate can fully meet.
Broken interview processes burn out both the interview team and the candidates, and nobody gets hired.
As a job seeker, you should find out as soon as possible whether you are stuck in a broken or stalled interview process.
In a healthy labor market, a job posting should not remain open for more than four weeks (six at the maximum).
If more than eight candidates have been interviewed with no decision made, the hiring process is likely broken and the company may not be a great place to work.
Interview team members who are frustrated with a stalled process will often tell you something is wrong and may even confess to wanting to leave the company.

Phantom Job Listing Syndrome occurs when a manager has already selected a candidate, writes a job description tailored to that person's résumé, posts it to satisfy corporate bureaucracy, and then hires the preselected person after cursory interviews.
Rapid churn of job descriptions on a company's website (coming and going every week or two) is a sign of phantom listings.
Cool, hot, growing companies face an oversupply of top candidates, so they have no fear about being unable to hire great people, which creates a particular risk for applicants.
A false positive in hiring (hiring a bad candidate) is far more costly and painful than a false negative (missing a great candidate), so companies are highly tolerant of false negatives.
Cool companies have draconian hiring processes not out of meanness but as a smart business decision necessitated by their popularity and the high cost of a bad hire.
Getting rejected by a cool company is a 'gravity problem'—you cannot control it; you can only play by their rules and hope you have what it takes.
A personal connection to people inside a cool company, built through prototyping conversations, can help you navigate the hiring process, though you still must go through it.
You should be brutally honest with yourself about your chances at a cool company and proceed with caveat emptor.

The 'Way It Should Be' for job descriptions focuses on candidates who connect their Workview to their Lifeview, exercise signature strengths, and possess high integrity, quick learning capacity, and intrinsic motivation—skills the company can teach.
Internet job descriptions are largely useless, filled with tortured language and superhero metaphors, and fail to address the deeper issues of why we work or what work is for.
Even useless job descriptions can serve as a potential starting point for a conversation with the institution they represent.
Awareness of the hiring process from the employer's perspective—writing job descriptions, reading résumés, interviewing—significantly increases your success rate in getting a job offer.
Empathy for the overwhelmed hiring manager is a crucial element of design thinking applied to a job hunt.
The key design reframe shifts focus from your need to find a job to the hiring manager's need to find the right person.
There is no perfect job that you perfectly fit, but you can make lots of jobs perfect enough.

exercises.title: Tailor Your Résumé to the Job Description Keywords
exercises.purpose: To increase the chance that your résumé is discovered in a company's HR keyword search and passes the initial 'fit' screening by matching the language of the job description.
steps: Read the first part of the job description and identify the words and phrases the company uses to describe the role and desired candidate.
Describe yourself in your résumé using the same words the company uses, so your résumé matches the keyword search.
If you possess the specific skills listed as required, add them to your résumé word for word.
If you do not have those exact skills, list very specific skills that are similar and find ways to describe them that might come up in a keyword search based on the job description.
In the screening phase, focus only on the skills match; do not mention other talents, multidisciplinary skill sets, or skills that are not part of the job description.
exercises.source_quote: So, to increase you chance of being discovered, use the same words that they used in the first part of the job description.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 4)

exercises.title: Rewrite Your Résumé Using Job Posting Keywords
exercises.purpose: To improve your chance of being discovered in a keyword search by matching the language of the job posting.
steps: Identify the specific words and phrases used in the job posting.
Rewrite your résumé to use those same words (e.g., say 'good written and verbal communication skills' instead of 'I'm a good writer and I communicate well').
Replace your own phrasing with the posting's phrasing (e.g., say 'passion for customers' instead of 'customer-centric attitude').
Be generous with self-description; do not be modest (e.g., include 'highly motivated' and 'creative').
materials: Your current résumé
The specific job posting you are targeting
exercises.source_quote: Rewrite your résumé using the same words used in the job posting. Say "good written and verbal communication skills," not "I'm a good writer and I communicate well"; say "passion for customers," not "customer-centric attitude."
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 5)

exercises.title: Match Specific Skills to Posting Language
exercises.purpose: To ensure your résumé surfaces in keyword searches by using the exact terminology of the job posting for required skills.
steps: Check whether you have a specific skill that is posted as required.
If you do have that skill, put it in your résumé exactly the way it is written in the Internet posting.
If you do not have that exact skill, find a way to describe your skill set that uses the same words that will be found in a keyword search.
materials: Your current résumé
The specific job posting you are targeting
exercises.source_quote: If you have a specific skill that is posted as required, put it in your résumé exactly the way it is written in the Internet posting. If you don't have that skill, find a way to describe your skill set that uses the same words that will be found in a keyword search.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 5)

exercises.title: Focus Your Résumé on the Job as Described
exercises.purpose: To increase the chance your résumé appears in a search and to position yourself as the answer to the company's specific needs rather than a generalist.
steps: Focus your résumé on the job as described in the posting, even if the description isn't very accurate.
Focus on the skills you can offer the company, using their words as often as possible.
Focus on what you can do for them, not on why this job works for you.
Do not appear to be a generalist or a multidisciplinary person on your résumé or in the first interview.
Focus on answering their needs.
Once you have reassured them that you have the skills required, move on to impress them with your depth.
materials: Your current résumé
The specific job posting you are targeting
exercises.source_quote: Focus your résumé on the job as described. Even if the job description isn't very accurate, this will increase the chance that your résumé will show up in a search.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 5)

exercises.title: Bring a Fresh Printed Résumé to the Interview
exercises.purpose: To demonstrate the care you put into designing your résumé, which is often the first time an interviewer sees it in physical form.
steps: Print a fresh, nicely printed copy of your résumé.
Bring that copy to the interview.
materials: A fresh, nicely printed copy of your résumé
exercises.source_quote: Always bring a fresh, nicely printed copy of your résumé to an interview. This will probably be the first time anyone will see the care you put into designing the darn thing.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 5)

exercises.title: Research the Job Posting Timeline
exercises.purpose: To quickly determine whether a job posting is stalled or operating normally, giving you an early signal that the interview process may be broken.
steps: Do some research to find out how long the job has been posted.
Compare the posting duration against the benchmark: in a good labor market, a job posting should never be open for more than four weeks (six at the max).
If the posting has been open well beyond that window, treat it as a warning sign.
exercises.source_quote: One way is to do some research and find out how long the job has been posted.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 6)

exercises.title: Find Out How Many Candidates Have Been Interviewed
exercises.purpose: To gauge whether the hiring process is functioning or is broken, and to pick up on the frustrations of the interview team that may reveal deeper problems at the company.
steps: Find out how many people have already been interviewed for the position.
Ask one of the people on the interview team directly; if they are in a stalled situation, they are frustrated and will probably tell you.
If more than eight people have been through the process and no decisions have been made, recognize that the hiring process is probably broken.
Treat this as a sign the company may not be a great place to work and consider walking away.
exercises.source_quote: Another is to find out how many people have already been interviewed.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 6)

exercises.title: Check Job Description Churn Rate for Phantom Listings
exercises.purpose: To detect whether a company is running Phantom Job Listing Syndrome, where job postings exist only to satisfy bureaucracy while a candidate has already been preselected.
steps: Find out how quickly job descriptions churn on the company's website.
If job descriptions are coming and going every week or two, this may indicate phantom listings.
If you applied to a posting and never heard back, or were given a cursory interview with no follow-up, consider that the listing may have been a phantom.
exercises.source_quote: One way to tell if this is happening is to find out how quickly job descriptions churn on a company's website.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 6)

exercises.title: The Hiring-Manager Reframe
exercises.purpose: To shift the job seeker's mental model from a self-centered 'I need a job' stance to an empathy-driven 'the hiring manager needs the right person' stance, making the job hunt more effective.
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'You should focus on your need to find a job.'
Replace it with the reframe: 'You should focus on the hiring manager's need to find the right person.'

Apply this reframe to your job-hunt activities (résumé, cover letter, interview preparation) by designing them around what the hiring manager needs to see in order to feel they have found the right person.
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: You should focus on your need to find a job.
Reframe: You should focus on the hiring manager's need to find the right
person.
exercises.chapter: 7. How Not to Get a Job (part 8)

key_ideas: There is no pre-existing 'dream job' waiting for you; you design it through a process of actively seeking and co-creating it.
Only about 20 percent of available jobs are posted (online or anywhere); the remaining 80 percent exist in the hidden job market.
The hidden job market is an insider's game accessible only to people already connected in the professional network where the job resides.
You cannot 'break into' the hidden job market as a job seeker, but you can enter it as a 'sincerely interested inquirer' who is looking for the story, not the job.

Life Design Interviews (prototyping) serve a dual purpose: they help you discover what kind of work you want to pursue AND they are the best way to access the hidden job market in your field of interest.
Authentic prototype conversations with people you are genuinely interested in meeting can lead to high-quality job offers and even a dream job.
A Life Design Interview is a prototype conversation focused on learning a person's life story, not on asking for a job.
More than half the time, the person you interview will initiate a job offer themselves once they see your genuine interest.

The open-ended question 'What steps would be involved in exploring how someone like me might become a part of this organization?' converts a story-gathering conversation into a job-pursuit conversation.
You should never ask 'Do you have any openings?' because the answer is probably 'No' and it limits possibilities to only what is currently listed.
Most job offers come through the hidden job market for unlisted positions, not through public listings.
Establishing a genuine connection and earning regard with the interviewee is a prerequisite before shifting the conversation toward a job.
Networking is absolutely necessary for lining up prototyping conversations and is not optional.
The negative stereotypes of networking (slick, self-interested manipulation) are the minority; most networking is simply asking for help and directions.
People function as 'The Other World Wide Web'—connections and referrals are the key mechanism for finding the right conversations.
