Effective networking involves reaching out to contacts, their contacts, and even strangers identified online, then asking whom you should be talking to.
Reframing networking as 'asking for directions' rather than 'hustling' removes the aversion and makes the process feel natural and reciprocal.
Helping another person (like giving directions) feels inherently good and is hard-wired into our DNA as social creatures.
Asking for referrals to people whose stories would be useful to hear is the professional equivalent of asking a local for directions.
'Network' is more noun than verb; the goal is to participate in a community's conversation, not to 'do networking.'
Every domain of human endeavor is held together by a web of relationships between real people, and that web is the only way to gain access to the hidden job market.
The most common way people are introduced across professional networks is by referrals from personal networks, which is communal behavior, not favoritism.
The Internet can transform a job search when used to find and reach out to people whose stories you want to hear, rather than simply browsing online job listings.

Leveraging LinkedIn and Google can dramatically increase your ability to find and reach people for informational conversations, turning the internet from a 'black hole' of applications into a powerful tool.
The 'nature of the work' is the top consideration for new graduates, yet it is impossible to truly know before you are very close to getting the job, making job descriptions a misleading filter.
Most job descriptions are dysfunctional and inaccurate, causing people to rule out opportunities before they even apply.
The most important reframe in career design is: you are never looking for a job, you are looking for an offer.
Shifting from 'looking for a job' to 'pursuing offers' changes your mindset from deciding whether to take an unknown job to being curious and proactive in generating opportunities.
A sustained effort of roughly 200 conversations over six months can yield multiple strong offers in a target field.
Reframe the job search from 'looking for a job' to 'looking for an offer,' shifting from judging to exploring and from negative to positive.
Authenticity matters: when you seek offers rather than one specific job, you can be genuinely curious instead of faking enthusiasm.
People hire people they like and find interesting, not résumés; the people most interested in us are the ones we are most interested in.
Curiosity is one of the most important life design mind-sets, central to prototyping conversations and experiences.
Pursuing 'latent wonderfulness' means staying open to the small chance that something interesting exists in an organization you may have prematurely dismissed.
You cannot know the true nature of a job from a faulty job description or preconceived notions; you must pursue the offer to find out.
The possibility that an opportunity might be a fit is enough to pursue it; you do not need certainty.
Genuine conversations and prototyping outperform mass applications in generating job offers and building a professional network.
Job searching is partly a numbers game: the more connections and prototypes you run, the more opportunities turn into offers.
There is no 'Job Charming'—the idea that a fully formed dream job is waiting to be found is a fairy tale.
You design your job the same way you design your life: by thinking like a designer, generating options, prototyping, and making the best choices possible.
Design thinking can be applied to getting a first job, transforming a current job, designing a next job, and integrating Workview and Lifeview.
A critical part of the process is learning to live into the choices you make.

exercises.title: Life Design Interviews (Prototyping for the Hidden Job Market)
exercises.purpose: To discover what kind of work you might want to pursue and simultaneously gain access to the hidden job market by entering professional networks as a sincerely interested inquirer rather than a job seeker.
steps: Stop applying for jobs through traditional methods (online postings, crafted applications).
Identify people in your field of interest whom you are genuinely interested in meeting.
Approach them as a 'sincerely interested inquirer—someone just looking for the story (not looking for the job).'
Conduct authentic prototype conversations (Life Design Interviews) with these people.
Use the conversations to learn what kind of work you might want to pursue and to build connections within the professional network.
exercises.source_quote: Kurt stopped applying for jobs and began conducting Life Design Interviews. He conducted fifty-six authentic prototype conversations with people he was genuinely interested in meeting.

exercises.title: Life Design Interview (Prototype Conversation)
exercises.purpose: To learn about a particular kind of work or role through a person's life story, helping you determine whether you want to pursue that kind of work yourself.
steps: Identify a particular kind of work or role you are curious about.
Reach out to people in that field and ask for their life stories rather than asking for a job.
Conduct the conversation with the goal of learning the story, not of getting a job.
Listen for the other person to initiate a job offer on their own (this happens more than half the time).
If they do not initiate, use the 'What steps would be involved…' question to shift the conversation toward exploring a role.
exercises.source_quote: all you're looking for from a Life Design Interview (functioning as a prototype conversation) is to learn about a particular kind of work or role to help you find out if you want, at a later date, to try to get a job doing that kind of work yourself

exercises.title: The 'What Steps Would Be Involved' Question
exercises.purpose: To convert a story-gathering conversation into a job-pursuit conversation in an open-ended way that invites possibilities beyond currently listed openings.
steps: Ensure you have established a connection and earned some regard with the person you are speaking with.
Express genuine fascination with the organization and the people you have met.
Ask: 'What steps would be involved in exploring how someone like me might become a part of this organization?'
Do NOT ask 'Do you have any openings?' or 'Wow—this place is great! Do you have any openings?'
exercises.source_quote: I wonder, Allen, what steps would be involved in exploring how someone like me might become a part of this organization?

exercises.title: Networking Reframe
exercises.purpose: To help the reader overcome the instinctive aversion to the word 'networking' by replacing a dysfunctional belief with a simpler, more natural mental model.
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'Networking is just hustling people—it's slimy.'
Replace it with the reframe: 'Networking is just asking for directions.'
Use the analogy of a stranger in a car pulling up and asking for directions to the nearest coffee shop to feel the natural, helpful impulse that networking taps into.
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: Networking is just hustling people—it's slimy.
Reframe: Networking is just asking for directions.

exercises.title: Networking Outreach for Prototyping Conversations
exercises.purpose: To guide the reader through the concrete process of building the web of contacts and referrals needed to arrange prototyping conversations in a target field or community.
steps: Reach out to your existing contacts to get connections and referrals to people you need to meet.
Reach out to your contacts' contacts (second-degree connections).
Identify and reach out to strangers online who are relevant to your target field or community.
Ask each person you contact whom you should be talking to—whose stories you should be getting to learn more about the field or area you are exploring.
exercises.source_quote: He had to reach out to his contacts, and their contacts, and he even had to reach out to strangers he'd identified online. Then he asked those people whom he should be talking to—whose stories he should be getting if he wanted to learn more about sustainable architecture in the Atlanta area.

exercises.title: Ask for Directions (Request Referrals)
exercises.purpose: To overcome the intimidation of reaching out to strangers in a new professional community by reframing the request as a simple, everyday act of asking for directions.
steps: Identify a professional community or industry you want to learn about (e.g., sustainable architecture in Atlanta, nanotechnology in Hong Kong).
Recognize that you do not need to know your way around the community in advance.
Ask a local (someone already in that community) for directions—i.e., request referrals to people whose stories would be useful to hear.
Treat the request as a normal, low-stakes interaction, the same way you would give or ask for directions on the street.
exercises.source_quote: Getting referrals to people whose stories would be useful to hear is just the professional equivalent of asking directions. So go ahead—ask for directions. It's. No. Big. Deal.

exercises.title: Use the Internet to Find and Reach Out to People
exercises.purpose: To leverage the Internet as a tool for building genuine connections with people whose stories and perspectives are relevant to your job search, rather than passively browsing job listings.
steps: Identify the people whose stories you want to hear in your target field or community.
Use the Internet to find those individuals (rather than searching for online job listings).
Reach out to them directly to initiate a conversation or request a referral.
exercises.source_quote: Use the Internet not to get online job listings but to find and reach out to the people whose stories you want to hear.

exercises.title: Reframe: From Job-Seeker to Offer-Pursuer
exercises.purpose: To shift your mindset from passively evaluating whether a job is 'right' for you to actively pursuing and generating multiple offers, which changes how you approach every stage of the career-design process.
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'I am looking for a job.'
Replace it with the reframe: 'I am pursuing a number of offers.'
Apply this new framing to every aspect of your search: which roles you consider, how you write cover letters and résumés, how you conduct interviews, and how you close the deal.
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: I am looking for a job.
Reframe: I am pursuing a number of offers.

exercises.title: The 20 Percent / 10 Percent Chance Question
exercises.purpose: To counter the tendency to dismiss an organization outright and to cultivate genuine curiosity by lowering the threshold for exploring a potential opportunity.
steps: Identify an organization you may have unnecessarily dismissed as not being a fit for you.
Ask yourself: 'Is there a 20 percent chance there's something interesting to me going on somewhere in this organization?'
If the answer is no, lower the bar and ask: 'Is there a 10 percent chance?'
If the answer to either question is yes, commit to finding out what kind of interesting offer you might be able to find in that organization.
Approach the organization with genuine curiosity and a willingness to pursue the latent wonderfulness, rather than trying to convince them you are the perfect fit for one specific role.
exercises.source_quote: What this means is that you ask yourself, "Is there a 20 percent chance there's something interesting to me going on somewhere in this organization? Is there a 10 percent chance?" If the answer is yes, then don't you want to find it?

key_ideas: In life design, being happy means you choose happiness.
The secret to happiness in life design isn't making the right choice; it's learning to choose well.
Being happy and getting what you want are about how you choose and how you live your choices once they're made, not about future risks or whether you picked the right alternatives.
All hard work can be undone by poor choosing—thinking wrongly about your choosing is more damaging than making the wrong choice, which is a recoverable risk.
Adopting a good, healthy, smart life design choosing process is critical to a happy outcome.
Many people guarantee an unhappy outcome by how they approach the design step of choosing.
Choosing well almost guarantees a happy and life-giving outcome while setting you up for more options and a better future.
Agonizing over choices is a time suck and is not part of the life design choosing process.

There is a four-step process for choosing, and understanding each step distinguishes good choosing (reliably happy outcomes, more future prospects) from bad choosing (preconditioning for an unhappy experience).
Step 1 (Gather and Create Options) involves generating ideas and alternatives using a curious mind-set and a bias to action versus overthinking.

Step 2 (Narrow Down the List) addresses the overwhelm of having too many options; the core issue is usually not a lack of information but the length of the list and one's relationship with all the possibilities.
Step 4 is to let go of unnecessary options and embrace your choice fully to get the most from it.
Building up a list of options may take weeks or months, and that is acceptable because you are designing your life.
Additional research, interviewing, and prototyping do not solve the problem of being stuck with too many options; the bottleneck is not knowledge.
The 'jam study' by Professor Sheena Iyengar shows that while more options attract attention, they drastically reduce the likelihood of actually making a purchase or decision.
Most minds can choose effectively between only three to five options; beyond that, decision-making ability wanes and can freeze entirely.
Modern culture idolizes having options, but the Internet and instant access to information have created a 'pandemic attack of too many options.'
If you have too many options, you actually have none at all, because you become frozen and unable to choose.
Options only create value in your life when they are chosen and realized; 'when an option grows up it becomes a choice.'
The solution to too many options is to narrow down and get rid of some, starting by grouping options into categories.
When you have too many options, you effectively have none, so you have nothing to lose by eliminating some.
You will not cross off the wrong option; if you do, you will realize it afterward.
The Pizza-Chinese Effect: you often don't know your true preference until an unwanted decision is made as a fait accompli, at which point your preference becomes clear.
If you cannot act on your narrowed list because you are in agony over the options you rejected, you must actively let them go before you can proceed.

If you truly cannot find meaningful distinctions among your remaining options, you have a can't-lose situation: all options are strategically worthwhile, and you should choose based on secondary considerations.
The goal of the decision process is to leave the store with some jam—i.e., to actually make a choice rather than remain paralyzed.
Emotional intelligence (EQ) is as important as, and in many situations more important than, cognitive intelligence (IQ) for achieving success and happiness.
The basal ganglia, part of the ancient base brain, guides our best choices and communicates through feelings and gut responses rather than words.
The 'wisdom of the emotions' is the collected experience of what has and hasn't worked in life, made available to us as feelings and bodily gut responses.
The default response of needing more information is counterproductive; it is the noisy, cogitating brain that blocks access to gut feelings on a decision.

Gathering good information (homework, notes, spreadsheets, comparisons, expert conversations) is important and is led by the prefrontal cortex's executive functions, but once that work is done, we need access to the emotional wisdom center to discern better choices.
Discernment is decision making that employs more than one way of knowing, including both cognitive knowing and affective/intuitive knowing.
There are multiple ways of knowing: cognitive, emotional, intuitive, spiritual, social, and kinesthetic.
The key to step three is making discerning decisions by applying more than one way of knowing, not relying on cognitive judgment alone.
Cognitive judgment is informed but not reliable on its own; the goal is to integrate all decision-making faculties rather than swap the brain for the heart or gut.
Emotional, intuitive, and spiritual forms of knowing are usually subtle, quiet, and even shy, requiring a slower, quieter approach to access.
Personal practices such as journaling, prayer, meditation, yoga, and Tai Chi help mature one's access to emotional, intuitive, and spiritual wisdom.
The best time to build emotional intelligence and spiritual maturity is when there is no decision at stake—during the 'off season,' not during the stressful 'playoffs.'
The best time to get ready for step three is months or years before the choosing.
The best time to start investing in your happiness is right now.
"Grok" means to understand something so deeply and completely that you feel you have become one with it.
The grokking technique allows emotional, spiritual, social, and intuitive forms of knowing to complement the dominant cognitive/evaluative mode of thinking.
When grokking a choice, you do not think about it from your current reality; you live calmly as the person who has already made that choice.
The fourth step in the decision-making process is not to agonize (second-guess, replay alternatives, wonder if you can redo it) but to let go and move on.
The mind-set about how to make a good decision is as important as which decision you actually make.
You cannot make 'the best choice' because you cannot know what the best choice was until all consequences have played out.
Agonizing—rehearsing the alternatives not chosen—drains satisfaction with the choice you made and distracts you from moving forward energetically.
Reversibility (keeping options open) is not conducive to establishing reliable happiness with a decision.
Simply being invited to reconsider and 'keep your options open' makes people doubt and devalue their choice, even if they never actually swap.
Letting go of your options is associated with greater and more reliable happiness with a decision.
The Paradox of Choice (Barry Schwartz): perceiving many unexplored options makes us less happy with the choice we actually make.
In the Internet-powered, globalized world, we are more capable of being unhappy with our choices than any prior generation.
Imagined choices don't actually exist because they are not actionable; we are designing a real and livable life, not a fantasy.
In life design, countless possibilities exist but we are not stymied by them; we explore a few, then take action.
Only by taking action can we build our way forward; letting go of unneeded options is key to choosing happiness.
Culling options to a short, manageable list (five max) and committing to the best available choice enhances success and satisfaction.
With prototype iteration, the stakes are low enough to adjust as you go before a significant investment is made.
Once a choice is made, embrace it and go with it rather than agonizing over roads not taken.
Direct your energy into living well the decisions you've made rather than fixating on decision regret.
The letting-go step relies primarily on personal discipline and winning the internal argument against rumination.
Use external supports—collaborators, teams, journaling—to stay anchored to the reasons behind your choices.
Happiness is not about having it all; it is about letting go of what you don't need.
A single mission can be pursued through multiple viable paths, and a backup plan does not diminish your primary ambition.
Overthinking a decision can trap you in an endless circular loop, described as a 'hamster wheel' of competing 'but…' objections.
'Grokking' a decision—imagining yourself actually living each option—reveals which path aligns with your values in a way pure analysis cannot.
Making a choice is not the same as letting go of it; implementation requires a separate, deliberate step.
Step four is called 'let go and move on' because merely trying to let go of a thought is nearly impossible; the secret to letting go is moving on.
A good decision is one you can live with, even when it involves a long, uncertain path, rather than one that simply avoids short-term discomfort.
Letting go is an inaction, and the brain resists inaction the same way nature abhors a vacuum.
The key to letting go is to move on and grab something else—put your attention on something, not off something.
The way out of a stuck state is into it: reframe from 'how do I let go of X?' to 'how can I move on and move into Y?'
Designers don't agonize, dream about what could have been, spin their wheels, or waste their futures by hoping for a better past.
Life designers see the adventure in whatever life they are currently building and living into; this is how you choose happiness.

exercises.title: Dysfunctional Belief Reframe
exercises.purpose: To shift the reader away from the belief that happiness depends on making the single 'right' choice, and toward the understanding that the quality of the choosing process matters more than the specific outcome.
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'To be happy, I have to make the right choice.'
Reframe it to: 'There is no right choice—only good choosing.'
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: To be happy, I have to make the right choice.
Reframe: There is no right choice—only good choosing.

exercises.title: The Life Design Choosing Process
exercises.purpose: To provide a structured, four-step framework for making career and life choices that leads to a happy, life-giving outcome rather than prolonged agonizing.
steps: Gather and create some options.
Narrow down your list to your top alternatives.
Choose.
Complete the fourth step (not agonizing; the specific fourth step is not revealed in this part of the chapter).
exercises.source_quote: In life design, the choosing process has four steps. First you gather and create some options, then you narrow down your list to your top alternatives, then you finally choose, and then, last but not least, you…agonize over that choice.

exercises.title: Write Your Workview and Lifeview
exercises.purpose: To generate insights about yourself and produce viable options for your life design.
steps: Write your Workview.
Write your Lifeview.
exercises.source_quote: to tell you (again) to write your Workview and Lifeview, to create mind maps, do your three Odyssey Plan alternatives, and prototype conversations and experiences.

exercises.title: Create Mind Maps
exercises.purpose: To visually generate and organize ideas, alternatives, and viable options for any area of your life.
steps: Create mind maps to explore options about where to engage with the world.
exercises.source_quote: to tell you (again) to write your Workview and Lifeview, to create mind maps, do your three Odyssey Plan alternatives, and prototype conversations and experiences.

exercises.title: Three Odyssey Plan Alternatives
exercises.purpose: To produce three distinct alternative life paths so you can compare and evaluate options before narrowing down.
steps: Develop three Odyssey Plan alternatives as part of your option-generating process.
exercises.source_quote: to tell you (again) to write your Workview and Lifeview, to create mind maps, do your three Odyssey Plan alternatives, and prototype conversations and experiences.

exercises.title: Prototype Conversations and Experiences
exercises.purpose: To test and explore options in low-stakes ways, building a curious, action-oriented understanding of what you want before committing.
steps: Prototype conversations and experiences related to your options, approaching them with a curious mind-set and a bias to action versus overthinking.
exercises.source_quote: to tell you (again) to write your Workview and Lifeview, to create mind maps, do your three Odyssey Plan alternatives, and prototype conversations and experiences.

exercises.title: Narrow Your Options List
exercises.purpose: To overcome choice overload by reducing a large list of options to a small, manageable set so you can actually make a decision.
steps: Look at your full list of options (e.g., twelve).
Cross out the options you want to eliminate (e.g., cross out seven).
Rewrite your list with only the remaining options (e.g., just five).
Proceed to Step 3 (Choose Discerningly).
exercises.source_quote: If you've got a list of twelve options, cross out seven, then rewrite your list with just the remaining five on it, and go to step three.

exercises.title: Burn the Rejected List and Take a Break
exercises.purpose: To help you release the emotional agony of losing eliminated options so you can commit to and act on your narrowed list.
steps: Burn the list of the options you rejected.
Put the entire decision down for a day or two.
Come back to your list of five later.
Treat that list of five as the list (not a shortened list).
Get going on your decision.
materials: The physical list of rejected options (to burn)
exercises.source_quote: Burn the list of the seven you rejected, put it all down for a day or two, then come back to your list of five later and treat that list as the list (not the shortened list), but do eventually get going.

exercises.title: Form and Maintain a Set of Personal Practices for Emotional and Spiritual Maturity
exercises.purpose: To develop and strengthen access to subtle, quiet, and shy forms of knowing (emotional, intuitive, spiritual) so that they are available and reliable when a real decision must be made.
steps: Choose a set of personal practices suited to you, such as journaling, prayer or spiritual exercises, meditation, or integrated physical practices like yoga or Tai Chi.
Practice regularly, month in and month out, rather than only when a decision is looming.
Prioritize practicing during your 'off season'—times when there is no pressure to perform and no choice at stake—so you can focus on just doing the practice and gaining strength and balance.
Avoid relying on these practices only during stressful, high-pressure moments (the 'playoffs'), because decision making is already stressful and the muscles need to be trained in advance.
Invest in your emotional intelligence and spiritual maturity well in advance—months or years before the choosing—so those faculties are strong and trained when it is decision or game time.
exercises.source_quote: we do encourage you to do so. The reason practices work to give you better access to your best wisdom in discerning a good decision relates precisely to the nature of such insights. Emotional, intuitive, and spiritual forms of knowing are usually subtle, quiet, and even shy.

exercises.title: Grokking a Choice
exercises.purpose: To let your emotional, spiritual, social, and intuitive forms of knowing express themselves and complement your cognitive evaluation when choosing among narrowed-down alternatives.
steps: From your narrowed-down list of alternatives, pick one (e.g., Alternative A) and stop thinking about it analytically.

For one to three days, choose to think that you are the person who has already made the decision to pick Alternative A. Treat Choice A as your current reality in everyday moments (brushing your teeth, sitting at a red light, etc.).
You may or may not mention the choice to others, but simply live in your head as the person in that alternative's reality.
After one to three days, take at least a day or two off to be your regular self and reset.
Repeat the same one-to-three-day grokking process with the next alternative (Alternative B), followed by another reset break.
Repeat again with the final alternative (Alternative C), followed by one more reset break.
Finally, do a thoughtful reflection on what each of those experiences was like and which one of those people you might most like to be.
materials: A narrowed-down list of alternatives (prepared in earlier steps)
exercises.source_quote: To grok a choice, you don't think about it—you become it.

exercises.title: Cull, Choose, and Build Forward
exercises.purpose: To overcome decision paralysis and the unhappiness caused by an overwhelming number of options by narrowing choices to a manageable set and committing to action.
steps: Get lots of options (explore and gather possibilities).
Cull the list down to a short and manageable size (five max).
Make the best choice you can, given the time and resources available to you.
Get on with it and build your way forward.
If using prototype iteration, adjust as you go before you reach a significant investment.
Once you make a choice, embrace it and go with it; when agonizing questions creep in, let go and move on.
exercises.source_quote: Do yourself the favor of getting lots of options, then culling the list down to a short and manageable size (five max); then make the best choice that you can, given the time and resources available to you, get on with it, and build your way forward.

exercises.title: The Letting-Go Step (Managing Decision Regret)
exercises.purpose: To help readers stop rehashing and ruminating on past decisions and instead direct their energy into fully enjoying the choices they have made.
steps: Keep your reframed understanding of decision making handy as a reference.
When tempted to rehash and ruminate, consciously win the internal argument with yourself.
Find a life design collaborator or team to help remind you why you made the choice or choices you did.
Make a journal entry about your decision, and reread it when you get confused.
Find what works for you to enable yourself to enjoy your choices fully.
materials: A journal or notebook for writing and rereading your decision entry
exercises.source_quote: This letting-go step relies primarily on personal discipline. Keep your reframed understanding of decision making handy, and be sure to win the internal argument with yourself when you're tempted to rehash and ruminate. Put in place the support you need to stick with it—find a life design collaborator or team to help remind you why you made the choice or choices you did; make a journal entry about your decision, and reread it when you get confused. Find what works to enable yourself to enjoy your choices fully.

exercises.title: Dysfunctional Belief Reframe: Happiness
exercises.purpose: To shift the reader's definition of happiness away from accumulation and toward release, reducing the pressure to 'have it all.'
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'Happiness is having it all.'
Replace it with the reframe: 'Happiness is letting go of what you don't need.'
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: Happiness is having it all.
Reframe: Happiness is letting go of what you don't need.

exercises.title: The Blue Horse Let-Go Demonstration
exercises.purpose: To demonstrate how difficult it is to simply 'let go' of a thought, illustrating why step four must be 'let go and move on' rather than just 'let go.'
steps: Put anything in your mind's eye except a blue horse.
Do not think about or see a blue horse.
Do not think about a spotted blue horse, a blue unicorn, or a blue pygmy pony with a red-and-white striped saddle and a pink ribbon on its tail.
exercises.source_quote: right now, put anything in your mind's eye except a blue horse. Whatever you do—do not think about or see a blue horse. No spotted blue horse. No blue unicorn. No blue pygmy pony with a red-and-white striped saddle and a pink ribbon on its tail.

exercises.title: The Blue Horse Attention Test
exercises.purpose: To demonstrate that 'letting go' (inaction) is far harder than 'moving on' (action), because the brain resists a void and will be 'stampeded' by the very thing you try to suppress.
steps: For the next sixty seconds, try to keep not seeing a blue horse.
Notice how your mind is 'stampeded by blue horses'—the very attempt to suppress the image makes it dominate your attention.
Reflect on the lesson: the key to letting go is not to focus on what to stop attending to, but to move your attention onto something else.
exercises.source_quote: Please keep not seeing a blue horse for the next sixty seconds.

exercises.title: Move Into, Not Away From (Reframing Practice)
exercises.purpose: To help a reader break free from a stuck, agonizing state by shifting the question from 'How do I let go of X?' to 'How can I move on and move into [the next thing]?', giving the mind permission to let go by filling the void with a new direction.
steps: Identify the worry, distraction, or 'hamster wheel' thought you are trying to let go of.
Instead of asking 'How do I stop thinking about X?', reframe the question: 'How can I move on and move into [the next thing I want to build]?'
Brainstorm concrete questions about how the new path can contribute to your goals (e.g., what skills, institutions, or experiences would be most relevant).
Imagine your way into the new path and generate prototype conversations and prototype experiences you could pursue in that role.

Notice how embracing what the new training or path can contribute gives you 'tons of ideas and lots of interesting questions to pursue,' which in turn gives your mind permission to let go of the old fixation.
exercises.source_quote: Andy realized that the way out of it is into it, and asked, "How can I move on and move into becoming a doctor?"

key_ideas: While you cannot avoid failure, you can become immune to the large majority of negative feelings of failure that burden your life needlessly.
Failure immunity is distinct from and more valuable than simply reducing your failure rate.
Grit or perseverance, as studied by Angela Duckworth, is a better measure of potential success than IQ, and failure immunity gives you grit to spare.
A life-design approach that embraces curiosity, prototyping, and a bias-to-action mind-set will cause you to 'fail by design' more than any other approach.
The fear of failure is tied to a binary perception of people as either successes or failures, as if an external judge will pass final judgment on one's life.
If you are designing your life, you cannot be a failure.
Prototypes and engagements that don't attain their goals are designed for learning, so they are not true failures.
Once you are living the ongoing creative process of life design, you can't fail; you can only be making progress and learning.
Failing more often at small, low-exposure learning experiences helps you succeed sooner at the big, important things.
The first level of failure immunity comes from a bias to action, failing fast, and being clear on the learning value of a failure so the sting disappears.
The second level, 'big failure immunity,' comes from the reframe that life is a process, not an outcome.
Life is always changing, and with each change comes a new design; life design is never done until you are.
Life design is compared to a set of dance moves for an ongoing dance that is never finished.
Everything in life is either a finite game (played by the rules to win) or an infinite game (played with the rules for the joy of keeping the game going).
Adopting an infinite-game mind-set—focusing on becoming more yourself and expressing your amazingness into the world—makes you truly failure-immune, because setbacks do not make you less of a person.
The being-versus-doing distinction is a false dichotomy; life design treats life as a wicked problem you never 'solve' but continuously improve at living.

Life design follows a productive cycle: start with who you are (being), generate ideas and try things (doing), make the best choice you can, and in the process grow into a more-like-you version of yourself (becoming), then repeat.
Finite and infinite games are not ranked; both are necessary and valuable in life.
Life is an infinite game with no winners or losers, not a finite game.
Failure is the raw material of success; setbacks can be reframed into growth.
A perfectly planned life that never surprises or challenges you is a boring life, not a well-designed one.
Embracing flaws, weaknesses, and major screwups is what makes life worth living and worth designing.
Repeated failure reduces the pain of losing, which in turn builds the courage to take new risks.
Reframing is not mere positive thinking but a design tool imperative to life design.
Everyone carries at least one redemption story in which a failure turned out to be the best thing that ever happened.
Each failure is a lesson, not a reason to stop trying; the point is how you keep running, not whether you finally win.
A lifetime of experience dealing with failure builds immunity that helps you accept and act on new crises without getting stuck.
When facing a major challenge, don't get stuck asking 'Why me?' or believing you have 'failed' at something; instead, prepare and execute a 'campaign' to address it.
Live your life, not just plan it—sometimes the smart plan and the life you want to live conflict, and you must choose to live.
Before making a bold decision, do prototype conversations with the people who will judge it to understand how they will perceive it.
The kind of people you want to work with will view boldness as a strength rather than irresponsibility.
Life is fragile, and a lifetime of 'success' does not insulate you from sudden, unplanned events.
Failure immunity means being immune from being misinformed by failure—you don't believe you are a failure, that failure defines you, or that your failures were truly failures.
Failure immunity enables a person to direct energy productively and to learn from adversity rather than being despondently confused about why bad things happen.
Turning a problem into an advantage allows you to design the best life possible in the face of adversity.
When an attempt fails, let go and quickly redirect efforts into an alternative plan rather than dwelling on the rejection.
Keep prototyping a desired career even after rejection: stay in touch with relevant people, build relevant work, and share it periodically.
Failures educate a person in the same way successes do; a failure-immune person will take whatever they get and keep 'failing their way forward.'
Failure immunity does not protect from the personal pain and loss of failure, only from the belief that failure defines your identity.
How well life feels is more about mind-set than current level of success.
Failure is the raw material of success, and the failure reframe converts that raw material into real growth.
Failures fall into three categories: screwups (simple mistakes), weaknesses (recurring failures from abiding failings), and growth opportunities (failures that didn't have to happen).
For screwups, the best response is to acknowledge, apologize, and move on.
For weaknesses, the best strategy is avoidance of triggering situations rather than trying to change your stripes.
Growth opportunities deserve the most attention because a fix is available and the failure doesn't have to happen again.
Building the habit of converting failures to growth leads to failure immunity.
A failure can be reframed by identifying the critical success factor—what could be done differently next time—and jotting down a single insight to put to work.

Not all failures are the same: some are one-time 'screwups' (unusual, preventable but not worth over-analyzing), some are persistent weaknesses you learn to work around, and some reveal a genuinely new insight.
Maintaining a failure log over time helps distinguish between patterns worth changing and quirks you simply live with.
A failure that is preventable but extremely unusual (e.g., a break-in during fumigation) can be accepted as a screwup rather than a lesson to act on.
Persistent weaknesses (like chronic procrastination) may have limited further learning; the goal shifts to working around them rather than eliminating them.
Sometimes a mistake reveals a blind spot in an otherwise strong skill (e.g., launching into a phone-call agenda without checking in, a habit that works in person but not on the phone).
A quick news-and-agenda check before getting to business—even on a phone call—can prevent costly oversights.
Failure reframing: analyzing what went wrong and what you learned turns a setback into productive insight rather than self-blame.
Life designers don't fight reality; they design their way forward no matter what happens.
A failed prototype still leaves you with valuable information about the state of the world at your new starting point.
In life design there are no wrong choices and no regrets—only prototypes, some that succeed and some that fail.
Life is about learning and playing the infinite game, not about winning and losing.
A little failure reframing can go a long way toward building failure immunity.
Converting failures to growth is a habit that should be practiced on a regular schedule.
A frequency of once or twice a month is recommended for this practice.

exercises.title: Reframe: Life Is a Process, Not an Outcome
exercises.purpose: To shift the reader's mindset away from judging life by its outcomes and toward embracing life as an ongoing, ever-changing process, thereby building 'big failure immunity.'
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'We judge our life by the outcome.'
Apply the reframe: 'Life is a process, not an outcome.'
Internalize that you are always growing from the present into the future, always changing, and with each change comes a new design.
exercises.source_quote:
Dysfunctional Belief: We judge our life by the outcome.
Reframe: Life is a process, not an outcome.

exercises.title: Prototype Conversations
exercises.purpose: To understand how relevant stakeholders (e.g., future hiring managers) will perceive a major life decision before you commit to it, so you can assess whether you can afford the risk.
steps: Identify the big decision you are considering (e.g., taking a year off, changing careers).
Identify the people who will be affected by or judge the decision (e.g., future hiring managers, businesspeople in your field).
Have conversations with those people to learn how they might view the decision.
Evaluate their feedback: can you afford the risk? Will the people you want to work with see the decision as boldness or irresponsibility?
Make your decision based on what you learned.
exercises.source_quote: He did some prototype conversations with businesspeople before he made his decision, because he wanted to learn how future hiring managers might look at that decision, and concluded that he could afford the risk, and that the kind of people he'd want to work with would view his post-cancer ski adventure as a demonstration of boldness rather than irresponsibility.

exercises.title: The Campaign Approach to a Major Challenge
exercises.purpose: To reframe a sudden, unplanned crisis (illness, loss, career setback) as a 'campaign' you prepare and execute, rather than something that has 'failed' you, so you can channel your energy into action instead of self-pity.
steps: Accept the reality of the situation quickly; do not get stuck asking 'Why me?'
Refuse to frame the event as a personal failure (e.g., 'I failed at being healthy').
Prepare a 'campaign'—a concrete plan of action—to address the challenge.
Execute the campaign, putting all your energies into the work ahead (e.g., surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or whatever the challenge demands).
Use the experience to learn how fragile life is and what matters to you.
exercises.source_quote: He didn't get stuck asking, "Why me?" Nor did he believe he had failed at being healthy. He was too busy getting another campaign prepared—this time, a campaign to beat cancer—and then using it.

exercises.title: Failure Reframe Exercise
exercises.purpose: A three-step process for converting failures into real growth, building the habit of failure immunity by regularly logging, categorizing, and extracting lessons from your mistakes.
steps: Log your failures: Write down when you've messed up. Look back over the last week, the last month, the last year, or create an All-Time Failure Hits List. Do this once or twice a month until you've established a new way of thinking.

Categorize your failures into three types: (1) Screwups—simple mistakes about things you normally get right; acknowledge, apologize as needed, and move on. (2) Weaknesses—recurring failures from abiding failings; your best strategy is avoidance of the situations that prompt them rather than trying to change. (3) Growth opportunities—failures that didn't have to happen, where the cause is identifiable and a fix is available; direct your attention here.

Identify growth insights: Examine your growth opportunity failures for an invitation to real improvement. Ask what there is to learn, what went wrong (the critical failure), and what fix is available.
materials: Paper or notebook for writing down failures
exercises.source_quote: Here's an exercise to help you do just that—the failure reframe.

exercises.title: Failure Log Reframe: Jot Down the Insight
exercises.purpose: To convert a specific failure into a concrete, actionable learning by isolating the critical success factor and capturing a single insight that could change the outcome next time.
steps: Identify what could be done differently next time (the critical success factor).
Look for an insight to capture that could change things next time.
Jot the insight down.
Put the insight to work.
materials: Something to write on (implied by 'jot it down')
exercises.source_quote: Look for an insight to capture that could change things next time. Jot it down and put it to work. That's it—a simple reframe.

exercises.title: Reframing Failure
exercises.purpose: To help the reader look back on recent failures, reframe them from self-blame into learning, and extract concrete growth insights that build failure immunity.
steps: Using the worksheet (or downloading it from www.designingyour.life), look back over the last week (or month or year), and log your failures.
Categorize them as screwups, weaknesses, or growth opportunities.
Identify your growth insights.
materials: The Reframing Failure worksheet (available at www.designingyour.life)
exercises.source_quote:
1. Using the worksheet below (or downloading it from www.designingyour.life), look back over the last week (or month or year), and log your failures.
2. Categorize them as screwups, weaknesses, or growth opportunities.
3. Identify your growth insights.

exercises.title: Converting Failures to Growth (Monthly Practice)
exercises.purpose: To build a consistent habit of turning failures into growth opportunities rather than letting them go unexamined.
steps: Build a habit of converting failures to growth by doing this once or twice a month.
exercises.source_quote: 4. Build a habit of converting failures to growth by doing this once or twice a month.

key_ideas: Great design is made great by a design team; true genius is a collaborative process.
Life design is an act of co-creation, not a solo heroic effort.
The mindset of life design differs fundamentally from career development, strategic planning, or life coaching, particularly in the central role of community.
Life design is intrinsically communal: 'we is always stronger than I.'
Wayfinding to build your way forward requires the contribution and participation of others; ideas and opportunities are not fetched for you on your behalf.
The dysfunctional belief 'It's my life, I have to design it myself' must be reframed to 'You live and design your life in collaboration with others.'
Your life design is co-created with a community of people you engage with in life.
Everyone you meet, engage, prototype, or converse with is part of your design community.
A few people become core collaborators, but everyone matters.
Co-creation is an integral aspect of a design point of view and a key reason design thinking works.
Your life design is not in you; it is in the world, where you discover and co-create it with others.
The ideas, possibilities, roles, and forms you will end up living do not yet exist and are waiting to be invented.
The raw material for invention lies in the hearts, minds, and actions of others, many of whom you have not yet met.
Traditional approaches fail because they rest on the false perception that you alone know the answers, have the resources, and know the right passion to follow.
The 'set some good goals and go get it' mentality is rejected as ineffective.
People often try to figure out their lives entirely on their own, standing alone in front of the mirror waiting for the correct answers.
Waiting to make a move until you are clear about the correct answers means you will be waiting a long time.

The people you have already engaged with throughout the book—conversations about values, Workview, Lifeview, Good Time Journal activities, ideation helpers, and prototype collaborators—constitute your team.
You may not have consciously recognized these individuals as a 'team,' but they are already part of your support structure.
You do not have to design your life alone; looking at the people around you reveals a team that is already in place.
Everyone participating in your life design effort in one way or another is part of your team.
Team members play different roles, and it is useful to name those roles.
Supporters are go-to people who care about your life, provide encouragement and useful feedback; not all friends are supporters and some supporters are not friends.
The number of supporters you have is largely a result of your personality, ranging from two or three to fifty or even a hundred.
Players are the active participants in your life design projects, especially ongoing work-related and avocational projects and prototypes.
Intimates include your immediate and close extended family members and your closest friends, who are most directly affected by your life design choices.
Certain individuals will appear in more than one of these roles.
Intimates are the most influential people in your life design, whether or not they are actively involved in the project.
You should at least keep your intimates informed about your life design work rather than leaving them out entirely.
Each intimate may need a different role in ideation, planning, and prototyping because some are too close, some have a preferred outcome, and some are ideal helpers.
Leaving intimates out of the process until the end seldom works out well.
The Team is a group of people who share the specifics of your life design project and track with you at regular intervals over time.
The most likely candidates for your team are among the people you invited to your feedback session to present and discuss your three alternative five-year Odyssey Plans.
Team members don't need to be your best friends; they just need to be willing to show up, be helpfully attentive and reflective, respect the process, and avoid being full of answers and advice.
A healthy team is more than two people and not more than six (including you); optimally, three to five people.
A pair (two people) places 100% of the response burden on one person and does not create enough diversity of opinion for true collaboration.
Three people introduce a much more active dynamic and allow a truly wide-ranging conversation.
Beyond six people, limited airtime causes fixed roles and personas to form, and the conversation shrinks.
Keep the team simple: its sole focus is supporting an effective life design—no more and no less.
Team members are co-creators in your life design, not therapists, financial advisers, or spiritual gurus.
The only role that truly needs to be defined is the team facilitator, who organizes meetings, scheduling, and communications.
The facilitator is a participant in the conversation, not a boss, referee, or leader.
The facilitator ensures everyone is heard, key ideas and suggestions aren't lost, and the team can determine direction when multiple issues arise simultaneously.
Stanford life design teams (called sections) operate under just four rules: Respectful, Confidential, Participative, and Generative.
Mentors play a very special role in a life design community or team and can greatly enhance the life design effort.
There is a clear distinction between counsel (helping you figure out what you think) and advice (telling you what the adviser thinks).
The phrase 'If I were you' is a reliable signal that you are receiving advice rather than counsel, because it really means 'If you were me.'
Advice is only truly useful if you happen to be identical to the person giving it.
Be cautious about taking advice from people who are essentially the same as you; seek diverse perspectives.
Before acting on advice, investigate the adviser's values, priorities, point of view, and the key experiences that shaped their conviction.
Two people can both be right about the same issue from different vantage points (e.g., the ER doctor and the motorcycling artist).
The critical question is not whether the advice is true, but how it relates to your specific situation.
Good advice on specialized matters (taxes, surgery) should come from people with indisputable expertise in that domain.
There is no single expert adviser for your life; what works for one person may not fit another.
What people call 'bad advice' is often good advice that simply didn't fit their situation.
Counsel is fundamentally different from advice: counsel is always helpful and clarifies your own thinking.
Good mentors are centered on giving counsel, which begins with asking questions to accurately understand you.
Good counselors ask the same question from different angles and restate what you've said to confirm understanding, showing they are focused on you, not themselves.
The value of a mentor's life experience lies in the breadth of their experience and their objectivity, which helps you see your own reality in a new way—not in borrowing their facts or answers.
Good mentors spend most of their time listening.
Mentors can offer reframings of your situation that help you generate new ideas and find answers that work for you.
Discernment involves employing multiple ways of knowing to make good decisions.
Mentors make a particularly valuable contribution to your discernment process when it's time to make important choices.
Important decisions create a 'noisy brain' full of competing issues and trade-off considerations.
A mentor helps you sort the noise into the big stuff, the small stuff, and the irrelevant stuff.
A good mentor resists telling you what to do and is explicitly cautious about the risks of overinfluencing you.
A good mentor may notice patterns in your reactions (e.g., lighting up when discussing a particular option) and gently point them out without dictating a choice.
Mentors come in many forms: lifelong mentors, topical mentors (parenting, finances, spirituality), and ad hoc or seasonal mentors (pregnancy, first managerial role, elderly parents, relocation).
There are no strict rules about mentoring; the key is to be on the lookout for people who can provide mentoring assistance.
There are many more people capable of giving good mentoring than there are 'master mentors.'
Many capable people don't think of themselves as mentors or aren't skilled in the practice of a mentoring conversation, but they are still mentors.
Being a good mentee is important; you do not need 100 percent master mentors to benefit from mentoring.
You do not need formal 'master mentors'; you only need 'mentor-capable people' from whom you can extract a mentor contribution.
You must be the initiator: identify the person, set up the time, and direct the conversation toward the areas where you want help.
The goal of the conversation is not to get the other person's advice on what to do, but to have them use their insights and experience to help you sort out your own thinking.
This approach is strikingly similar to setting up a prototype conversation (as described in chapter 6).
Extracting a mentor contribution from someone in your life is 'surprisingly easy' to do.
You can build your own stable of mentors rather than waiting for a single master mentor to appear.
A mentor's role in this context is to help sort out the majors from the minors of a challenge, not necessarily to give advice.
Community is more than sharing resources or hanging out; it is showing up and investing in the ongoing creation of one another's lives.
Community should be treated as an ongoing practice, not just something you engage in when making big plans or starting new things.
Identifying sustaining practices that keep you growing and enjoying your well-designed life is an important part of the formula, and community is a key piece.
The sincere, respectful listening and support experienced in a Life Design Team are habit-forming and lifegiving.
A 'community' in Life Design is an ongoing experience, distinct from an ad hoc Life Design Team.
Historically, people found communities organically through faith traditions, extended families, or shared careers/avocations.
Today, most people lack a ready-made community to return to regularly for meaningful life conversations.
A community is a group of people that shares specific attributes, beginning with Kindred Purpose.
Healthy communities are about something—not just getting together to get together.
The most effective communities have an explicit mission that keeps them directed and moving.
A community's core purpose acts as a 'North Star' that pulls members back to 'why we're here,' even when activities veer into social or recreational territory.
A community must meet regularly to sustain a consistent, ongoing conversation where members can pick up where they left off.
Participation in the community should become a practice in and of itself, not just an ad hoc gathering for a project.
A life lived in a community-supported way is a better designed life.
Shared ground—such as common values or a shared point of view—helps strengthen a community beyond a kindred purpose.
Commitment to total honesty (a 'No BS' rule) and willingness to try new things and 'do the work' are examples of shared ground.
Members can use reflective exercises to revise the potential content of their eulogy, recognizing that as long as you're alive it's not too late to change.
Explicit shared ground keeps a group together, sustains conversation, and serves as a means of establishing priorities and mediating issues.
A community is at least in large part about the people, not merely the content or process.
A group can have a clear purpose, shared ground, and a regular meeting schedule (e.g., a book club) without constituting a true community.
A true community requires members to be engaged in one another's lives and to know one another personally.
A community does not have to be made up entirely of intimates, but it requires some level of personal disclosure among members.
What makes an effective community is not having people with the right expertise or information, but people with the right intention and presence.
It is most helpful to be with people who are trying to connect the dots and live in coherence with themselves and the world in an honest way.
Being around someone sincerely turning into their best self is more encouraging and impactful than being in community with someone who shares your interests but isn't sincerely present.
You don't need everyone to strip emotionally naked, but you want a group in which you're going to be known and you're going to know others at a level where you feel like you're all in this together.
The critical distinction is between commentators (people talking about ideas about their lives) and participants (people actually talking about their lives).
The goal is to find or create a community of participants.
Life Design is a journey that is more enjoyable and effective when undertaken with others rather than alone.
A Life Design Team should consist of three to five people who are supporters, intimates, mentors, or possible mentors, ideally people also actively designing their own lives.
All team members should understand the life design process and the team roles and rules before working together.
The team should commit to meeting regularly and actively to co-create a well-designed life as a community.

exercises.title: Identifying Your Team
exercises.purpose: To help the reader recognize and name the different roles people play in their life design effort, so they can understand who is supporting, actively participating in, or most directly affected by their work.
steps: Think of everyone participating in your life design effort in one way or another as being part of your team.
Identify your Supporters: the go-to people you can count on to care about your life, whose encouragement keeps you going and whose feedback is of real use.
Identify your Players: the active participants in your life design projects, especially your ongoing work-related and avocational projects and prototypes—the people you actually do things with.
Identify your Intimates: your immediate and close extended family members and your closest friends, who are most directly affected by your life design choices.
Note that certain individuals may appear in more than one of these roles.
exercises.source_quote: Everyone participating in your life design effort in one way or another should be thought of as being a part of your team, but there are different roles to be played, and it's useful to name them.

exercises.title: Apply the Four Team Rules
exercises.purpose: To establish a safe, productive, and constructive environment for members of a life design team or section to share and collaborate.
steps: Adopt the rule that all interaction in the team must be Respectful.
Adopt the rule that all interaction in the team must be Confidential.
Adopt the rule that all interaction in the team must be Participative (no holding back).
Adopt the rule that all interaction in the team must be Generative (constructive, not skeptical or judging).
exercises.source_quote: As far as rules go, we use just four in our Stanford teams (which we call sections).

exercises.title: Find Mentors for Your Life Design Effort
exercises.purpose: To enhance your life design effort by having a few mentors participating with you in your life design community or team.
steps: Seek out a good mentoring experience if you have not had one.
Invite a few mentors to participate with you in your life design effort.
exercises.source_quote: we urge everyone to try to find it. Your life design effort will be greatly enhanced if you've got a few mentors participating with you.

exercises.title: Investigating the Adviser's Perspective
exercises.purpose: To help the reader critically evaluate received advice by understanding the background, values, and experiences that shaped the adviser's recommendation, so the reader can judge how well it fits their own situation.
steps: Identify the adviser's values and priorities.
Determine the adviser's point of view on the matter.
Discover what key experiences informed the evolution of the adviser's conviction about that specific advice.
Assess how the advice relates to your own circumstances before deciding whether to act on it.
exercises.source_quote: If you're getting advice, try to find out the adviser's values and priorities and point of view, and what key experiences informed the evolution of her conviction about that advice.

exercises.title: Extracting a Mentor Contribution
exercises.purpose: To leverage the experience and insights of a 'mentor-capable person' in your life as an informal mentor, helping you sort out your own thinking on a specific challenge without requiring a formal mentor relationship.
steps: Identify someone who you think can serve you as a mentor (a mentor-capable person).
Find a way to spend some time with the person (e.g., suggest buying them a cup of coffee).
Direct the conversation to the areas in which you want help.
Let the person share relevant stories and experiences first (e.g., endearing and scary moments from their own experience).
Ask the person not to tell you what they would do, but to use their insights and experience to help you sort out your own thinking on your specific situation.
Frame the request by acknowledging their practiced perspective (e.g., 'you've got a practiced father's ear') while noting your situation may be different from theirs.
exercises.source_quote: When you identify someone who you think can serve you as a mentor, find a way to spend some time with the person and direct the conversation to the areas in which you want help. Specifically, ask him not so much to tell you what he'd do as to use his insights and experience to try to help you sort out your own thinking.

exercises.title: Building a Stable of Mentors
exercises.purpose: To create a reliable, diverse network of mentors who can help you sort through challenges, so you are not dependent on a single master mentor.
steps: Ask a potential mentor to help you sort out the majors from the minors of what you are dealing with.
If the mentor veers into giving advice, listen respectfully and then come back to your original request.
If the mentor does not get the role, accept it without loss and try someone else.
Repeat the process with different people to build up your own stable of mentors.
exercises.source_quote: This way, you can build your own stable of mentors without having to wait for one of the master mentors to appear on the horizon.

exercises.title: Community as an Ongoing Practice
exercises.purpose: To sustain growth and enjoyment in a well-designed life by making community a regular, ongoing practice rather than a one-time event tied to big plans.
steps: Show up and invest in the ongoing creation of one another's lives within your community.
Engage in community not just when making big plans or starting new things, but as a regular, ongoing practice.
Identify what sustaining practices will help keep you growing and enjoying your well-designed life, recognizing community as an important piece.
exercises.source_quote: we highly recommend it as an ongoing practice, not just when making big plans or starting new things.

exercises.title: Play Dead / Eulogy Reflection
exercises.purpose: To help community members confront how they are perceived and to decide whether they want to revise the potential content of their own eulogy.
steps: Ask a member to play dead.
The other members talk about that person as if they were at his funeral.
Each member listens and then decides if he wants to revise the potential content of his eulogy.
exercises.source_quote: crazy exercises—such as asking someone to play dead, then talking about him as if they were at his funeral. As long as you're alive it's not too late to revise the potential content of your eulogy, so each member listens and can then decide if he

exercises.title: Commentators vs. Participants Reflection
exercises.purpose: To help the reader identify what makes a community truly effective by distinguishing between groups where people merely discuss ideas about their lives and groups where people are genuinely present and engaged with their own lives.
steps: Think of the different groups you've participated in over the years.
Identify groups in which the people were talking about ideas about their lives (commentators).
Identify groups in which the people were actually talking about their lives (participants).
Recognize that a community of participants is what you're looking for.
exercises.source_quote: Think of the different groups you've participated in over the years. You can probably think of groups in which the people were talking about ideas about their lives, and groups in which the people were actually talking about their lives.

exercises.title: Building a Team
exercises.purpose: To assemble a small, committed group of supporters, intimates, and mentors who will walk alongside you in the Life Design process and co-create a well-designed life together.
steps: Make a list of three to five people who might be a part of your Life Design Team, thinking of your supporters, your intimates, your mentors or possible mentors. Ideally, these will be three to five people also actively engaged in designing their lives.
Make sure everyone has a copy of the book (or buy books for everyone), so all the members of your team understand how life design works and have reviewed the team roles and rules.
Agree to meet regularly and actively to co-create a well-designed life as a community.
materials: A copy of the book for each team member (or budget to purchase copies)
exercises.source_quote: Make a list of three to five people who might be a part of your Life

key_ideas: There is no perfect pie; it is virtually impossible on any given day to devote yourself equally to all important areas of life.
Balance happens over time, not within a single day.
Life design happens over time.
Balance is a myth that causes grief and heartache.
Life design is about being able to answer the question 'How's it going?'.
A well-designed life is a verb, not a noun—it is an ongoing process, not a finished product.
You never finish designing your life; it is a joyous and never-ending design project.
Life is about more than a paycheck: it is about mattering to someone, contributing to the world, loving, living with purpose and meaning, and having fun.
The goal is to design your life so that in retrospect, those closest to you would say you had a 'pretty evenly sliced pie.'
Life designing is an ongoing process, not a one-time event; even after a major transition, you keep building your way forward.
Wayfinding is both the method for finding your life design and the method for living it day to day.
Design is not merely a technique for solving problems and projects—it is a way of living.
Human-centered design (HCD), pioneered at Stanford in 1963, keeps humanity at the center, making it well-suited to life design because life is a decidedly human enterprise.
Life design only addresses the question of *how* to design your life, not *what* life you should live or *why* one life is better than another.
A well-designed life can look radically different from person to person; Tim's choice to prioritize play, love, friends, and happiness over promotions and money is a valid and balanced design.
Unlearning things is often harder and more important than learning things.
Good design releases the best of what was already there waiting to be found and revealed, rather than turning you into a different person.
The foundation of the design methodology is an explicitly human process applied iteratively, offering both an approach to conceiving the life you want and a way to live it.
The five mind-sets of life design are: (1) be curious, (2) try stuff (bias to action), (3) reframe problems, (4) know it's a process (awareness), and (5) ask for help (radical collaboration).
The five mind-sets can be applied virtually anywhere, on any given day, and the opportunities to live into them are endless.
Applying any of the mind-sets can help you get unstuck and take progressive next steps in your life design.
A well-thought-out life design strategy does not require work to be the most important thing.
Endless curiosity is key to a well-designed life; nothing is boring to everyone.
A bias to action eliminates being stuck, worrying, and over-analyzing.
Reframing is a change in perspective, and almost any design problem can use a perspective switch.
Awareness of the process prevents frustration, getting lost, and giving up.
Radical collaboration means you aren't alone in the process.
The five mind-sets should be kept as an active orientation to how you're living, used in both life design implementation and the innovation process.
Beyond the five mind-sets, two additional elements are essential for a well-designed life: your compass and your personal practices.
Your compass—built from your Workview, Lifeview, and values—provides the foundation for answering 'How's it going?' and tells you whether you are living a coherent, aligned life.
The compass should be revisited at least annually and recalibrated, because while primary views stay fairly constant, specifics, nuances, and priorities do change.
Investing in and committing to personal practices (yoga, meditation, poetry writing/reading, prayer, etc.) is the single most important recommendation for sustaining a well-designed life.
Even a small effort in personal practices can bring great results by educating your emotions and maturing your discernment.
Modern cultures generally excel less at disciplined personal practices than traditional Eastern cultures, making this an area of great weakness.
A well-designed life is built from a personal set of intentional practices that animate creativity, connection, and presence.
Practices should be prototyped and customized to fit the individual rather than copied wholesale from others.
Life Design Interviewing can reveal unexpected career fits by connecting existing strengths to new contexts.
Journaling and working on one's compass can help a person recognize and trust their inner voice, potentially revealing a hidden calling.
Adopting a mind-set of curiosity can reframe complaints into opportunities for redesign.
Slowing down (e.g., walking instead of cycling) allows for more intimate engagement with nature and relationships.
Reframing your perspective—shifting focus from the 'what' and 'how' to the 'why' and 'who'—can transform your experience without changing your external situation.
You do not need to change your circumstances to reinvent yourself; a shift in state of mind is sufficient.
You do not need to use every tool in the book; taking up the challenge, getting unstuck, and building forward is what matters.
Life design is ultimately a way of life that transforms how you look at and live your life.
The end result of a well-designed life is a life well lived.
The goal is to be able to answer 'How's it going?' satisfyingly for yourself.
Life design involves perpetual curiosity and constant evolution as you move through different roles and seasons.

exercises.title: Imagining Your Perfect Pie
exercises.purpose: To help the reader visualize an ideal, balanced distribution of time and energy across the major areas of life, establishing a personal benchmark for what 'well-designed' looks like.
steps: Imagine a day cut into perfectly equal pieces of pie—one slice for career, one slice for play and fun, one slice for family and friends, one slice for health.
Ask yourself: 'What is your perfect pie?'
exercises.source_quote: Imagine a day cut into perfectly equal pieces of pie—one slice for career, one slice for play and fun, one slice for family and friends, one slice for health. What is your perfect pie?

exercises.title: Assessing Your Actual Pie
exercises.purpose: To ground the reader in reality by comparing the ideal pie to how they actually spent their day, highlighting areas that need more design thinking and less worry.
steps: Reflect on how much of your day today you actually spent having some fun.
Reflect on how much time you spent advancing your career.
Reflect on how much time you spent nurturing your relationships.
Reflect on how much time you spent taking care of your health.
Reflect on how much time you spent prototyping what's next.
Ask yourself: 'What does your pie really look like?'
exercises.source_quote: Now, how much of your day today did you actually spend having some fun? Advancing your career? Nurturing your relationships? Taking care of your health? Prototyping what's next? What does your pie really look like?

exercises.title: Dysfunctional Belief Reframe: Finishing Life Design
exercises.purpose: To challenge the belief that life design is a one-time project with a finish line, replacing it with the understanding that life design is an ongoing, joyful process.
steps: Identify the dysfunctional belief: 'I finished designing my life; the hard work is done, and everything will be great.'
Reframe it: 'You never finish designing your life—life is a joyous and never-ending design project of building your way forward.'
exercises.source_quote: Dysfunctional Belief: I finished designing my life; the hard work is done, and everything will be great. Reframe: You never finish designing your life—life is a joyous and never-ending design project of building your way forward.

exercises.title: Designing Your Way Forward
exercises.purpose: To help you get unstuck on specific problems in your life design project by applying one of the five mind-sets with the support of peers.
steps: Identify two or three things in your life design project that you are stuck on—things that are going nowhere fast.
Gather with two other students (or collaborators).

Ideate for four minutes on your stuck problem while the two others help you apply any one of the five mind-sets (curiosity, bias to action, reframing, awareness, or radical collaboration) as a way to get unstuck.
Use the insights generated to take progressive next steps.
materials: Two other students or collaborators
exercises.source_quote: We run an exercise in our classes called Designing Your Way Forward, in which we have our students identify two or three things in their life design project that they are stuck on, things that are going nowhere fast. We then ask them to ideate for four minutes on that stuck problem with two other students, who will help them apply any one of the five mind-sets as a way to get unstuck.

exercises.title: Be Curious
exercises.purpose: To cultivate endless curiosity as a key to a well-designed life by asking probing questions about anything, even mundane tasks.
steps: Pick something you're encountering (even taxes or washing dishes).
Ask: What would someone who's interested in this want to know?
Ask: How does it work?
Ask: Why do they do it that way?
Ask: How did they used to do it?
Ask: What do experts in this field argue about and why?
Ask: What's the most interesting thing going on here?
Ask: What don't I get about what's happening here?
Ask: How could I find out?
exercises.source_quote: Be Curious. There's something interesting about everything. Endless curiosity is key to a well-designed life. Nothing is boring to everyone (even doing taxes or washing the dishes).

exercises.title: Try Stuff
exercises.purpose: To adopt a bias to action so you stop being stuck in worry, analysis, and pondering, and instead just do things to learn.
steps: Ask: How can we try this before the day is out?
Ask: What would we like to know more about?
Ask: What can I do that will answer that?
Ask: What sorts of things are actionable, and if we tried them, what might we learn?
Act on the answer before the day is out.
exercises.source_quote: Try Stuff. With a bias to action, there is no more being stuck—no more worrying, analyzing, pondering, or solving your way through life. Just do it.

exercises.title: Reframe Problems
exercises.purpose: To shift perspective on a design problem by examining your current vantage point and redescribing the problem through alternative lenses.
steps: Ask: What perspective do I actually have?
Ask: Where am I now coming from?
Ask: What other perspectives could other people have? Name them, and then describe the problem from their perspective, not yours.

Redescribe your problem using reframe lenses: Your problem is actually very small. Very easy to fix. An opportunity more than a problem. Something you can just skip entirely. Something you actually don't understand at all yet. Not your problem. And how will it look a year later?
