exercises.source_quote: Reframe Problems. Reframing is a change in perspective, and almost any design problem can use a perspective switch.

exercises.title: Know It's a Process
exercises.purpose: To build awareness of where you are in the process so you don't get frustrated, lost, or give up, and to externalize worries to clarify next steps.
steps: Ask: What are all the steps behind you and in front of you that you can imagine?
Ask: Is what's on your mind actually germane to the step you're on now?
Ask: Are you on the right step, or are you ahead of or behind yourself?
Ask: What happens if you don't think more than one step ahead?
Ask: What's the worst thing that can happen? How likely is it to happen, and what would you do if it did?
Ask: What's the best thing that can happen?
Write down all the questions, worries, ideas, and hopes that you have.
Ask yourself if you know what to do next.
Notice: Does it feel different now?
materials: Paper or notebook for writing down questions, worries, ideas, and hopes
exercises.source_quote: Know It's a Process. Awareness of the process means you don't get frustrated or lost, and you don't ever give up.

exercises.title: Ask for Help
exercises.purpose: To practice radical collaboration by connecting with supporters, communities, mentors, and an ongoing help-seeking journal so you aren't alone in the process.
steps: Find a supporter you can talk to about what you're in the midst of—right now.
Tell this person your situation for five minutes.
Ask for five minutes of feedback and discussion.
Notice how you feel now (regardless of what your supporter said—just talking to someone other than yourself).
Build a team or create a community around your work.
Identify all the different groups and constituencies involved in what you're working on. Are you connected to and in conversation with all of them? If not—get going.
Keep an ask-for-help journal in which you jot down the questions you want help on, and keep it handy.
Each week, identify some people who can help you with some of the journal entries and reach out to them.
Journal answers and results from your helpers.
Find a mentor.
materials: An ask-for-help journal (notebook or digital document) kept handy for jotting down questions and recording answers
exercises.source_quote: Ask for Help. Radical collaboration means that you aren't alone in the process.

exercises.title: Call Your Mother
exercises.purpose: A brief, immediate prompt to reconnect with a loved one and take a small, meaningful action in your life.
steps: Call your mother.
exercises.source_quote: Call your mother (she'd love it—you know she would).

exercises.title: Revisit and Recalibrate Your Compass Annually
exercises.purpose: To stay on top of how your Workview, Lifeview, and values are shifting over time, ensuring you remain aligned and continue creating meaning in your life.
steps: Set aside time at least once a year to revisit your compass.
Re-examine the great big organizing ideas of your Workview and Lifeview.
Review your values and how they inform your answer to 'How's it going?'
Note any changes in specifics, nuances, and priorities since your last review.
Recalibrate your compass to reflect your current thinking and values.
Use the updated compass to check whether who you are, what you believe, and what you're doing are in adequate alignment.
exercises.source_quote: We urge you to revisit your compass at least annually, and recalibrate it. This will help you revitalize the creation of meaning in your life.

exercises.title: Commit to Personal Practices
exercises.purpose: To sustain a well-designed life by educating your emotions and maturing your discernment through disciplined, regular practices that yield daily benefits.
steps: Choose one or more personal practices suited to you (e.g., yoga, meditation, poetry writing/reading, prayer).
Invest in and commit to these practices as a regular part of your life.
Refine your participation over time through disciplined, ongoing engagement.
Even a small effort is encouraged, as it can bring great results.
exercises.source_quote: Perhaps the most important recommendation we can give you to sustain a well-designed life is to invest in and commit to some personal practices of the variety we described in chapter 9.

exercises.title: Morning Meditation and Daily Affirmation (Bill's Routine)
exercises.purpose: A concrete example of a daily personal practice that nourishes the practitioner by combining meditation with a grounding affirmation and a mental review of the day ahead.
steps: In the morning, while shaving, do a short meditation.
Recite the daily affirmation: 'I live in the best of all possible worlds. Everything I do today, I choose to do.'
Recount in your mind everything in front of you that day.
Remind yourself that all of it is something you choose to do.
exercises.source_quote: Bill is nourished by a morning meditation (done while shaving) and the daily affirmation he referred to on his health dashboard: "I live in the best of all possible worlds. Everything I do today, I choose to do."

exercises.title: Weekly Painting and Drawing Practice
exercises.purpose: To animate the creative brain and experience the pure joy of making art as a regular part of life.
steps: Dedicate significant time each week to painting and drawing.
Approach the activity as a way to animate your creative brain and experience pure joy.
exercises.source_quote: He also now dedicates significant time each week to painting and drawing to animate his creative brain and experience the pure joy of it.

exercises.title: Weekly Complex or Gourmet Meal
exercises.purpose: To do something creative that others can share in, combining creativity with community.
steps: Plan and prepare at least one complex if not gourmet meal each week.
Share the meal with others.
exercises.source_quote: And he makes at least one complex if not gourmet meal a week, to do something creative that others can share in.

exercises.title: Daily Silent Meditation (Centering Prayer)
exercises.purpose: To recenter oneself in the love of God through a brief daily practice of silence.
steps: Set aside twenty minutes each day for silent meditation (technically 'centering prayer').
Use the time to recenter yourself in the love of God.
exercises.source_quote: Dave works to spend twenty minutes a day in silent meditation (technically "centering prayer") to recenter himself in the love of God.

exercises.title: Weekly Poetry Reading in the Body
exercises.purpose: To learn how to feel a poem physically rather than only reading it intellectually, deepening emotional and sensory engagement with language.
steps: Read poetry at least once a week.
Try to learn how to feel the poem in your body, not just read it in your head.
Optionally, have a trusted partner or spouse curate your poetry assignments.
exercises.source_quote: He also now reads poetry at least once a week, trying to learn how to feel the poem in his body, not just read it in his head.

exercises.title: Weekly Slow Walk in the Hills
exercises.purpose: To slow things down and see nature more intimately by trading a faster, thrill-based exercise for a contemplative walk.
steps: Once a week, forgo the speed and thrill of road cycling as exercise.
Instead, walk in the hills for at least four miles.
Walk with a companion (e.g., spouse) and, if applicable, dogs, to share the experience.
exercises.source_quote: And he forgoes the speed and thrill of road cycling as exercise once a week to walk in the hills for at least four miles with Claudia and the dogs, to slow things down and see nature more intimately.

exercises.title: Build and Prototype Your Own Set of Practices
exercises.purpose: To encourage the reader to design a personalized collection of daily and weekly practices that help them live their own well-designed life.
steps: Identify areas of your life where you want more creativity, connection, or presence.
Build and prototype your own set of practices to find what works for you.
Iterate until the practices help you live your own well-designed life.
exercises.source_quote: we hope you will build and prototype your own set of practices to find what works for you and helps you to live your own well-designed life.

exercises.title: Life Design Interviewing
exercises.purpose: To discover unexpected career or project fits by interviewing people in fields of interest and connecting your existing strengths to new contexts.
steps: Decide to get good at being lucky by starting Life Design Interviewing.
Interview people in roles or industries that interest you.
Listen for how your existing strengths (e.g., organizing, categorizing) map onto the work they do.
Network your way toward opportunities where your strengths and curiosity stand out.
Allow the Life Design Interview to evolve naturally into a job or project conversation.
exercises.source_quote: she decided to get good at being lucky and started Life Design Interviewing.

exercises.title: Journaling to Discover Your Inner Voice
exercises.purpose: To recognize and trust your own inner voice, which may reveal a hidden identity or calling (e.g., as a writer or poet).
steps: Commit to a regular journaling practice.
Pay attention to what the journaling reveals about who you are and what feels lifegiving.
Recognize when the practice points to a deeper identity or vocation.
Act on the insight (e.g., pursue formal training or a new career path).
exercises.source_quote: She found journaling lifegiving and eventually recognized that the reason journaling had become so important to her was that she is a writer—a poet, actually.

exercises.title: Work on Your Compass
exercises.purpose: To develop personal practices that help you recognize and trust your own inner voice, aligning your choices with your authentic direction.
steps: Work deliberately on your compass (your internal sense of direction and values).
Develop personal practices that help you recognize and trust your own inner voice.
Use the insights gained to make larger life decisions.
exercises.source_quote: Janine really worked on her compass and developed personal practices that helped her to recognize and trust her own inner voice.

exercises.title: Reframe Complaints with Curiosity
exercises.purpose: To shift from a fixed, complaining stance to an open, curious one that opens up new possibilities for redesign.
steps: Identify a complaint or frustration in your life.
Adopt the mind-set of curiosity toward that complaint.
Reframe the complaint as a question or signal pointing toward a design opportunity.
exercises.source_quote: Donald used the mind-set of curiosity to reframe his complaint

key_ideas: The book 'Designing Your Life' (DYL) was developed at Stanford and is intended as 'a gift for everyone.'
The authors emphasize 'radical collaboration' as a guiding principle in building the Life Design Lab and the book itself.
The book is centered on 'life design' and draws on real people's stories (with names changed) to illustrate how life design works.
The authors' approach was shaped by mentors at Stanford, including Bob McKim, Bernie Roth, and Jim Adams, who taught them to 'bust conceptual blocks.'
The book required a collaborative team—writer, agent, and editor—to transform a class script into a publishable work.
Jim Adams' 2007 challenge ('I don't know how you guys could actually teach this stuff!') spurred the authors to figure out how to teach life design effectively.
The publishing process involved significant rethinking: the first draft was 'essentially a boring script of our class,' and the agent helped them discover what book they actually had to offer.
The author expresses deep gratitude to Vicky for her unwavering confidence, vision, and inspiration in bringing the book to life.
Even experienced designers benefit from external inspiration and encouragement from collaborators.
A collaborator's unconditional commitment and belief in a project can serve as a renewable source of energy for the creative team.
Life can be approached as a design problem, drawing on design thinking methodologies.
People who make an explicit connection between their work and something socially meaningful are more likely to find satisfaction and better able to adapt to stresses and compromises.
The concept of 'flow' (optimal experience) is relevant to understanding how people engage with their activities.
The AEIOU framework (Actors, Environments, Interactions, Objects, User needs) is a design research tool for needfinding.
The 'odyssey years' refer to the period roughly between ages 22 and 35, a time of exploration and identity formation.
Parallel prototyping leads to better design results, more divergence, and increased self-efficacy.
Positive psychology, especially the work of Martin Seligman, underpins many of the book's ideas and exercises.
The 'odyssey years' represent a period of improvisation that is a sensible response to modern conditions.
Candidates are increasingly powering the economy, shifting recruitment power away from employers.
Emotional intelligence and the 'wisdom of the emotions' are relevant to choosing happiness.
Happiness can be 'synthesized' rather than simply found, and the paradox of choice complicates decision-making.
Grit and self-control are important traits, and the distinction between finite and infinite games frames how one approaches failure.
